"THIS IS LIFE." ".1 have planned much work for my life," she said,: A girlish creature, with golden hair, And bright and winsome as she was fair. "The days are full till he comes to wed; The clothes to buy, and the home to make A very Eden, for his dear sake." But cares soon come to the wedded wife; She shares his duties, and hopes, and fears, Which lessen not with the waning years; For a very straggle, at best, is life; If we knew the burdens along the line' We should shrink to receive this gift divine. Sometimes, in the hush of the evening hour, She thinks of the leisure she meant to gain, And the work she would do with her hand and brain. " I am tired to-night; I am lacking power To think," she says; I must wait until My brain is rested, and pulse is still." Oh! woman and man, there is never rest; Dream not of leisure that will not come Till age shall make you both blind and dumb. You must live each day at your very best; The work of the world is done by a few; God asks that a part be done by you. Say oft, of the years, as they pass from sight, " This, this is life, with its golden store; I shall hive it once, but it comes no more." Have a purp:2e, qnd do with your utmost might; You will finish your Vg ork on the other side ; When you wake in His lineness, satisfied. —Conyregationalist.

Josh Billings. A country grocer has sworn out a warrant against his wife for pouring a gallon of molasses over his head. She should have heaped coals of fire upon him instead of dosing him with taffy in its crude condition; but her revenge was sweet anyhow. "Your honour," said a lawyer to the Judge, "every man who knows me knows that I am incapable of lending my aid to a mean cause." "That's so," said his opponent: the learned gentleman never lends himself to a mean cause—he alwa7s gets cash down." A gentleman who had tarried late at his club found his wife in a high state of nervousness awaiting his return. She said, " Hers I've been waiting and rocking in the chair till my head spins round like a top !"—" Jess so, my dear, where I've been," responded he. "I think itsh in the at- mosphere." .It is said that if you count a hundred slowly when any- thing happens to disturb you you will not swear. This Es probably the reason that most men count a hundred slolly when they slip on an orange skin and are about to blend with the sidewalk. At dinner, one evening, Miss Joy was most amiable to a very young captain who sat next to her. He was mightily pleased at being on such nice terms with a live actress. Suddenly she said, in her artless, pretty trimmer, "I am to take a boy's part in a new play, and I have been watching you ever since we were introduced. You don't mind, do you ? "—"lt made a fellym feel such a foul, don't you know," remarked the aaptain as he told the story in confi-

dance. to me. It was while in the North Woods that the following is said to have happened. A party were camping at Clear I Pond. One of them strayed off by himself in quest of fun and something to shoot at. He became lost, and as the shades of night began to creep over the landscape he began to get troubled, then seared; and as he was scared he ever ant anon would shout, "Men lost! man lost!" And as the • despening shadis of night drew on he became frantic, and made the welkin ring again and again with the despairing cry of "Man lost! man lost!" Just as the day faded into night, and he shrieked the despairing cry like the wail of the lost, a horned owl, perched on a tree near by, with all the wisdom of his race, cried out, "Who, who, a who, whoo!" The man stopped and started, and then in answer to the query, answered, "Jim —, of Rochester, you fool, you." Professor Agassiz took a very neat way once of disposing of the pretensions of a professional " mejum." He had denounced spiritualiats as knaves, and received a call from Rome the big Pan3andrnm-with-a-little-round-button-on- top of, mediume, who aeked him to attend a spiritualist séance that wee to he held in Boston. Agassiz ordered him out of his house. Home observed that this was a strange reception indeed on the part of a philosopher. "Well," said Agassiz, "what shall I see at your seance ?" "You will see,'' replied Home. "legs and arms moving about the room, and some of them will touch you." "Mr. Home,"anewered Aglesiz, "I will attend your meetingeand I will aid you to clear up the mystery of those floating limbs. I have a sword; it so happens that it was recently sharpened. That sword I will bring with me, and I will cut at the legs and arms." Home thanked him and withdrew. The next day Agassiz drove up to the hall where the seance was to be held. The doors were shut, but on them there was a pla- card announcing in large letters that no seance would take place, as Mr. Home had unexpectedly been recalled to New York. A FRENCH KING OF MADAG kSCAR.—It is well known that the claims of France to a protectorate over Madagaiscar are not of yesterday; bat probably few people have heard that she at one time gave a king to a province of that island. The romantic history of King Samuel Tuley Noro, as told by Robert Drury, an English captive in Madagascar at the beginning of the eighteenth century, is as follows : About 1620 the French formed a settlement at Port Dan- -Phine in the district of Anosy, in the extreme south-east of Igada'gasear. This encroachment led to a war, in the course of whieh the native king was killed and his son carried away to France. The French prevailed, and occupied the country until their dominion was terminated by a general massacre. Some years afterwards a French vessel, being in great straits for water and provisions, was compelled to put into Port Dauphine. The captain, knowing the hostility of the natives, pretended to be an envoy from the French king on a mission of atonement and reconciliation. His overtures were accepted, his wants were supplied, and the Queen of the country, mother of the young prince who had been car- ried away, paid a visit to the ship. While she was on board she watched the seamen bathing, and, observing one whose skin was much darker than that of his companions, took it into her head that he was her long-lost son. The captain, fearing her anger, if she were disappointed, prompted the sailor to humour her, and the latter having no objection to reign in Madagascar, came readily into the idea. The marks on hie person were verified, his reminiscences of his infancy were pronounced accurate, and he was duly installed as monarch under his own name of Samuel, with the addition of Tuley Noro, a compound of his presumed Madagascar I name with a word signifying return. His reign was long I and prosperous, and he always treated the French with par- tiality until a drunken sailor having told the natives that they were deceived, Samuel put him to death and forbade French vessels to visit Port Dauphine for the fature.—St. James's Gazette. WATcHING A TUMBLE BUG.—" 'ramble bug" is the com- mon name given by Americans to a species of beetle. It is a very clever creature, and how ingenious it is will be seen from a sketch furnished by a tourist to the Boston Congre- gationalist. The tourist had gone to a resort on the Dela- ware River, between the States of New Jersey and Pennsyl- vania, known as the Water Gap. He says :—" Having gone out, like Isaac, to meditate in a field at eventide, my atten- tion was arrested, not by approaching camels, but by a smaller moving object on the ground at my feet. The field was a sloping pasture, crested with a grove, falling away into a valley at the right, skirted with a rough country road on the left, having a pebbly surface, and carpeted with a soft, short, fine weed, with strawberry-vine-like leaves. How it was that in the midst of the extending scenery my eye caught this moving object at my feet I do not know; bat there it was, and a 'very curious object it proved to be. It was a round ball of earth, about an inch in diameter, as perfectly round as if it had been turned in a lathe or shaped in a mould. This earthen ball, two black beetles, half an inch long, Perhaps, were busily engaged in rolling down the slope. This they did by an ingenious and amusing division of labour. While one of them stood perched upon the top 0.: the ball, treading it along under his feet like the acrobat icr the picture, the other pushed the ball from the up-hill sic; with his hind feet, standing up against the ball head downs yard. with his fore feet resting on the ground; and between them they made the ball roll along at a pretty pace. ps, sr so small an object the surface of the ground was very nneva m, and the obstacles in the way were many and considerable ; but the beetles were vigorous and enterpria. ino-, and not. king stood long in their way. They rolled I tar burden a, round the pebbles and over the weeds, and minded never a jolt nor a tumble. By and by, as I bent ' 'e 'the to take alarm, and, changing oeer them, they their coursin`rollea the ball up hill a little way, and then k by a great loop until they had re- around upon its tree direction at a greater distance than gained their original 'gable intruder from Boston. Gibbs writes to Land :—A lugubrious lady (or gentle- man) in the Quarterly Review has recently re-echoed the wail of the three "wise judges" at Reading. I venture to infer that this anonymous champion if of the softer sex, from the blending of a half plaintive, half angry " bleating" tone, natural to an otherwise lady-like or lamb-like intellect when suddenly plunging out of its depth, and from a deli- cate disregard of strict logic, a lather loose accuracy as to fact, and an occasional "derangement of epitaphs." It will be painfully remembered for many a bad year by thousands whom it will ruin, that the three learned judges deputed by the R.A.S.E., and speaking (for the nonce) in the name of the" People of England," preached from this high platform the safe, easy, and comfortable doctrine of despair! They wasted some 10 or 14 weeks of time, £2,000 in money, and a great deal more temper than they could safely spare, in ad- judicating upon the rival claims of a crowd of puffing fan- makers, and in showing us how not to save our harvests in wet seasons. Out of those many weary weeks they gave one half-My for a scornful trial and pre-judged condemna- tion of a system that had cost 28 years and £lO,OOO to per- fect and prove. The writer in the Quarterly repeats, with evident gusto, the sneer of the judges as to the "strong evi- dence of confidence in Mr. Gibbs' system evinced at Read- ing by the quantity of black and ill-smelling hay which we saw in the rick-yard." She ignores (as they did) the well- known fact that this black hay was the result of an attempt to make it by the stack-cooling process, and not by my system at all. She also ignores (as they did) the other well- known fact that whilst they were humorously pronouncing harvest saving in bad weather impossible, at that very time, and within half an hour's rail of them, the Duke of Northumberland's harvest-saver was securing, and had secured, so large a harvest on his Grace's estates and on the farm of one of the tenants, that it more than sufficed to re- coup the whole first coat of the machinery in a single sea- son. She ignores also (as they did) the authenticated and voluntary evidence given by Mr. Fuller, of Weston Park, to the effect that he also hadsavedthe entire filet cost of a £350 machine in two seasons; of similar authentic and incontro- vertible evidence from Mr. Charles James Morris, of Wood- e,aton Manor, Stafford, that he had repaid himself the first cost of £4OO in three seasons; and the voluntary public acknowledgments of the value of this resource from men of the highest position in half the counties of the kingdom. A man writing on a subject of such vital importance to the whole nation, and wishing to arrive at an impartial con- clusion, would have consulted your columns and those of your contemporaries to see what had really been done since that unlucky "muddle," and would have seen that at that very Reading, where harvest-saving had been pronounced impossible, the authorities had immediately decided to pur- ehasie another harvest-saver (like the one condemned as useless). This was a conflict of judgment so very curious that it will, I trust, afford some amusement to your readers. The machine was put to the absurdly inadequate test of a few hours' work on rubbish so vile and foul with filth that it hardly deserved the name Of grass at all, and because it did not convert this rubbish into fine hay, the whole system was instantly, finally, and eternally condemned. But the fun of the whole thing lies in this—that the first and only effect of this eternal condemnation was the immediate de- cision of the Council, who had watched its former results, seen this sham trial, and heard that condemnation, to be- speak another machine of exactly the same type, price, and form for this present season. When one comes to think of it, this was rather a heavy "snub" for the judges, and one can hardly wonder that such important and dignified per- sonages should feel coneiderably sore at having their non possumus torn to shreds under their august noses, and their interdict calmly set aside as soon as it was uttered. A gentleman inquired of a humble Hibernian the reason why his countrymen are so apt to make bulls. " I'll tell you that, your honour," replied Paddy. "We never make bulls in our own language; it is when we speak English that we do it—so, your honour, they are English bulls not Irish. A young lady, in reply to her father's question why she did not wear rings upon her fingers, said, "Because papa, they hurt me when anybody squeezes my hand." "What business have you to have your hand squeezed ?" "Cer- tainly none; but still you know, papa, one would like to keep it in squeezing order." The father couldn't see it. FORCE OF biAGINATION.—One day I gave a dinner after dissecting a Mississippi aligator. The guests congregated. The meal commenced with excellent soup. "How do you like the soup ?" I asked, addressing a famous gourmand of the day. "Very good, indeed," answered the other; "turtle, is it not? I only ask because Ido not find any green fat." I shook my head. "I think it has somewhat of a musky taste," said another—"not unpleasant, but peculiar !" "All aligators have," replied I, "the cayman peculiarly so which I dissected this morning !" There was a general rout of the whole guests. Everyone turned pale. Half-a-dozen started up from the table. Two or three ran out of the room, and only those who had stout stomachs remained to the dose of the entertainment. See what imagination is; if I had told them it was turtle, or ter- rapin, or bird's nest soup, salt water amphibia or freet, or the gluten of a fish from a maw of a sea bird, they would have pronounced it excellent and their digestion been none the worse—such is prejudice! It was simply mock turtle, made from as good a calf's head as ever wore a coronet.— Buckland's Curiosities of Natural History.

The plague of larrikinism, more extensive than at the time when Anthony Trollope wrote of it, is also awaiting the attention of the social and moral reformer. Melbourne and its suburbs (and in the same way every large town in the colonies, and oftentimes the smaller, too) has its gangs of impudent young blackguards, the incarnation of mischief and rowdyism, who set the police utterly at defiance and vie with other in acts of vandalism and disorder. The old country street rough is a novice in audacity as compared with the Victorian larrikin.

In however many and diverse methods the higher life may be aimed' at in Victoria, the colony is, however, sadly, in need, like many other parts of the world, of moral im- provement. As to tippling, which is often mentioned as one of the special vices of Victoria and the Australian colonies, I do not think that this is any worse than in the parent country. Over indulgence in intoxicants has ob- viously its peculiar dangers in this semi-tropical climate. And if current reports are to be believed, a very large quan- tity of the liquor that is vended here is about as unwhole- some as it is possible to make it. The colonial brewers and distillers get the dis-credit as a rule for producing the offensive stuff, but if the truth could be known it is not un- likely that the sin could be with justice laid at other people's doors. Gambling is a vice which is undoubtedly alarmingly prevalent in the colony. A popular phase of this spirit is seen in the multitude of sweeps and raffles which even the churches do not hesitate to resort to in a wholesale manner—under the agreeable title of "art unions "—when funds are required to be raised. The racing sweeps are, so far at any rate as my knowledge extends, quite unique. They are variously described, but the pre- vailing appelations given to them in the advertisements by which the promoters announce them to the public are— " Consultations " and "Seances." In some instances the price of a share is a half-crown, but more often a pound. A few weeks before any great race meeting in Australia these sweeps are opened, to be filled with amazing rapidity by all classes who invest in the hope of securing a winning number. The sweeps known as "Millers" have the reputa- tion of being genuine and honestly managed, but there are many others known to be unmitigated swindles. All are equally illegal and equally mischievous, but the police are apparently not able, or if able are unwilling, to suppress them. Profanity should be mentioned as a very prevalent vice in the Australian colonies. Among the young, the "natives" and pre-eminently among the larrikin class, swearing is in- deed fearfully common. Men who ought to feel heartily ashamed of themselves for setting such an example to the young and rising generation, garnish their ordinary conver- sation with expletives which would become wearisome by their monotony, if objectionale on no other ground. There is one word ending with a "y" which is the favourite, and this, I am bold to assert, you will hear more often in Vic- toria, the extent of population taken into account, than anywhere else. There is so much that is pleasing and to the credit of the people who are engaged in building up this great nation in the Southern Seas, that to mention a failing of this character is naturally very unpleasant. But candour compels,
MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

A special meeting of the subscribers to the Parliamentary Fund of the Manchester Ship Canal was held on Tuesday afternoon at the Manchester Town Hall, and was largely attended.—Mr. Daniel Adamson occupied the chair, and was supported by the Mayor of Salford, the Mayor of Hey- wood, and others. A statement of accounts was presented, and showed that the Committee had received up to date £46,7881 and had spent £47,500. Their assets were esti- mated at £12,000, and their liabilities at £13,000 to £14,000i including the fourth call upon the subscribers. The Com- mittee were of opinion that another application to Parlia- ment would be successful. They were strongly of opinion, that steps should be at once taken to secure the consent of the Conservators of the Mersey to the plans for the improve- ment of the estuary, and to obtain the necessary fends for a second application to Parliament. The Chairman moved the reception of the report and state- ment, which was seconded by Mr. Alderman Barley, and passed.—The Mayor of Salford (Mr. Alderman lilts- , band) proposed a resolution expressing regret that after the 1 searching inquiry by the Select Committee of the House of Commons the committee of the House of Lords should, have rejected the measure.—Cantain Stott seconded the motion, which was adopted.—Mr. Alderman Harwood proposed another resolution, declaring that the necessity and advan- tage of connecting the city of Manchester and the adjoining districts with the sea had been established beyond con- troversy, and empowering the Provisional Committee to promote a bill or establishing a ship canal in the next session.—Dr. Mackie (Warrington) seconded the motion, which was passed unanimously.—During the meEting it was pointed out by the Chairman that much of the expense already incurred would not have to be repeated. About £5,006 had already been promised, and he believed £25,000 more would cover the cost of another application to Parlia- ment. On Thursday the General Purposes Committee of the Manchester City Council adopted a report of the Parliamen- tary Sub-committee with reference to the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. Referring to the rejection of the bill by the Lords' Committee after the prolonged inquiry in the House of Commons, the Sub-committee speak of this as a striking instance of the hardship of the present mode of procedure on private bills, and they suggest that in future a single in- quiry before a joint committee of both House-$, should , suffice.
A poll has been tal,;en at Accrington on the question of grocers' licenses, with the result that four-fifths of the bour,eholders have vet cd aping the renewal of licenses.
NTELLIGENCE.
The International Corn and Seed Market was opened at

Vienna on Monday. The Sultan has sent to the Princess of Montenegro a set of diamonds worth £20,000. A New York telegram says there are indications of a failure in the crop of winter apples throughout the entire co untry. _ _
Martial law has been proclaimed in the Hungarian die- Acts in which armed peasants have during the last four or . _ _ _ _

tire days plundered houses belonging to Jews. THE DEATH OF THE QUEEN OF MADAGASCAR is re- ported in a telegram received at the headquarters of the London Missionary Society. It is reported from Rome that the Comte de Chambord has bequeathed a legacy of considerable amount to the Pope. _ . _
It is understood that the Countess will enter a convent.
Twenty-two workmen have been killed and 17 injured by the falling of the scaffolding employed in building a new castle for the King of Bavaria on the island in the Chiem Lake.
THE MURDER OF CAREY.—At a meeting of Irish-Ameri- cans held at Nashville on Monday a large sum of money was collected for the defence of O'Donnell, the murderer of
James Carey. FATAL FIRE IN BOSTON.—A fatal fire has occurred in a tenement kouse at Boston. There were a large number of

residents in the building, but all managed to escape except five, who were burnt to death. ANTI-JEWISH RIOTS have again broken out in Western Hungary and at Z.,la Egersseg. Twenty soldiers are re- ported to have been killed and wounded in defending the Jews from the violence of the mobs. 111 E SOUDAN.—News has been received from the Soudan that affairs in that province are not progressing satisfac- torily, as some of the chiefs who had received a free pardon from the Khedive had returned to the camp of the False Prophet. PROPOSAL TO KIDNAP PRESIDENT ARTHUR.—A Utah paper contains a sensation story of a plot conceived by a band of outlaws to capture President Arthur and his party auring their tour in Yellowstone district and hold them

for ransom. MADAGASCAR: RELEASE OF MR. SHA.W.—From Mada- gascar we learn that the proceedings against Mr. Shaw, the missionary, have resulted in a decision that there was no ground for the charges against him. Mr. Shaw has, there- fore, been set at liberty. VoLCANIC ERUPTION.—A violent volcanic eruption has occurred in Java, resulting in an immense destruction of property. Several bridges have been destroyed, the rivers have been made to overflow by the rush of the sea inland, and it is known toat one village has been washed away. THE RIOTS IN ALEXANDRIA.—Twenty-three of the men charged with having organised riots in Alexandria were tried by court-martial on Tuesday, 13 of them being con- demned to be banged. Two of the prisoners were acquitted, and the remainder were sentenced to various terms of penal sevitude. BRIGANDAGE IN TURKEY.—A rumour has reached Con- stantinople that the brigands have murdered the persons whom they seized at Floria. Ghazi Mehemid Pasha, governor of Salonicanvho was recently captured by brigands, has been rescued owing to the energetic steps taken by the Turkish authorities. ZULULAND.—According to a private despatch there ap- pears to be no prospect of peace in Zululand until Cetewayo has completely overcome all the other chiefs, or they have destroaeed him, unless, indeed, England interferes with a strong hand, and insists upon all parties remaining in peace on the ground allotted to them. FamterE RELIEF IN INDIA.—The Government has decided to start famine relief works in the Northern provinces, owing to the drought prevailing there. Eight thousand persons will be employed in the distriets,of Hissar and Sirsa. A broad gauge railway will be construed from Ihansi to Manicupore, in the district of Banda. Tun' WEST COAST OF AFRICA. According to intelli- gence received at Lisbon the King of Dahomey has set the garrison of the Portuguese fort at Whydah at liberty on Ureic entering into an agreement not to cede the place to England. It is reported that Mr. Stanley has closed the navigation of the Upper Cong2flor general commerce. Crum AND PERU.--4 sanguipeary battle has been fought between the Per'uvian and Chilian forces at Huamachuca, on the 10th ult. After a long conflict the Chilians obtained the mastery, flriving their opponents from the field in utter confusion, with a loss of 800 or 1,000 men. The victors also captured eleven guns, 800 rifles, a standard, :and large quantities of ammunition. POLITICAL ARRESTS IN RUSSIA.—A number of political arrests are reported to have recently taken place in Russia. Amongst the number are said to be a naval officer and an artillery officer. A lieutenant of artillery and five soldiers were taken into custody at Cronstadt, several students at Tiflis, and four lads, disguised as the servants of an officer, at Kamm. Some journalists and others have also been placed under arrest. NEW ZEALAND.—A petition to the Queen, ponying for a redress of grievances, is now being signed by the members of all the Maori tribes in New Zealand. Among other things which the natives ask for is permission to establish a Maori Parliament, subordinate to the general assembly of tl* colony. The petition, which has already received 6,000 signatures, will probably be brought to England before the close of the year. SHOCKING ACCIDENT IN THE ALPS.—A terrible accident to an Alpine tourist is reported from the Grisans. Mons. Cornprez, an French gentleman from Cannes, and member ot a climbing club, bad organised an ascent on the Her- nima Mountain, taking with him three guides. In as- cending a difficult point the party, it appears, slipped, and M. Combrez was killed. One of the guides was seriously hurt, but the others were uninjured. THE UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT AND WASHINGTON. —The property of Wakefield; Westmoreland County, Vir- -inia, where Geo. Washington was born, haebeen purchased ty the United Sates Government. It is about 36 miles from Washington City, is 20 acres in extent, and is a portion of the property owned by Washington's grandfather. Con- gress has, moreover, voted 33,000 dollars to erect a moms- rnent upon the spot where the " Father of his Country " was born. FRENCH VICTORY OVER THE ANNAMITES. —lnformation has been received by the French Minister of Marine of the bombardment of the forts and batteries situated on the Hu6 river, and the occopation of the works by the French forces, after a brilliant land attack. The operations were carried out on the 18th, 19th, and 20th instant. The Anna- mites are reported to have lost about 700 killad and a large number of wounded. The French had several men slightly, wounded. A truce had been granted by the Admiral. Ac- cordine, to a telegram published by the Paris Temps; the King of Annam and the French plenipotentiaries have drafted a treaty confirming the protectorate of France over Annam. Under this treaty Annain agrees to pay Francnan indemnity for the cost of the war, the French to retain pos- session of the forts at the mouth of the Hue river till the indemnity be paid.

The co-operative stores at North Ormesby, Middles- borough, we, e entirely destroyed by fire early on Thursday morning. The damage is estimated at £7,000. The pier at Aberystwith caught fire on Thursday after- noon in the centre. The flames spread rapidly, but by great exertions the fire was got under in about an hour. THE NEW DOCKS AT PnEsToer.—The Preston Corpora- tion on Thursday authorised the carrying forward of certain preliminary works in connection with the new docks at Preston and the opening of the Ribble navigation Mr. aarlick, the present mayor, was appointed engineer to the works from the expiration of his year of office. SINGULAR FATAL FALL AT BOLTON.—Whilst leaning ever a small wicket gate with a child in his arms, Patrick Manning, an Irish labourer, who lived with his son in Can- , non-street, Bolton, was suddenly precipitated don n a flight of steps through the woodwork giving way. The child was uninjured, and Manning's skull was fatally fractured, and the coroner's jury returned a verdict of accidental death. THE CONSERVATIVE SPLIT AT P2ESTON.—The breach which for some time has existed in the Conservative camp , at Preston has been healed, and at a meeting of the repre- aentatives of each side on Wednesday evening an arrange- ment involving the recognition of the parliamentary statue ,of Mr. W. E. M. Tomlinson was come to. Hitherto his op- ponents have been the Conservatives of the Guildhall-street Club, and the arrangement now made embraces their acquiescence. UNFORTUNATE TE2MINATION 01 A PLEASURE DRIVE.: On Sunday evening last an alarming occurrence took plaee in Gladdenhey. brow, Downall Green, where a trap con- taining several persons was upset. It is stated that the party came from Stubshaw Cross, and their intention was to have a pleasure drive in a trap belonging Mr. John Wood, the horse also being owaed by that gentleman. At the spot indicated, however, the vehicle was from some cause upset. and the occupants were severely shaken, though none re- ceived serious injury. POACHING AFT,RAY.—A desperate poaching affray. oc- curred about one o'clock on Thursday morning on Mr. Wharton's estate, Skelton Castle,Cleveland. Four poachers were observed bf three gamekeepers and a policeman in the act of snaring rabbits. On an attempt being made to arrest them, they turned upen the keepers, and a struggle, which lasted half an hour, ensued. The poachers being armed with stones and bludgeons offered strong resistance; one of the gamekeepers had his area broken and a policeman his fingers severely bitten. Two of the men escaped, but Robert White and James King, who bore marks of the severe en- counter, were arrested. EXPLOSION OF BLASTING POWDER.—A shocking explo- sion of blasting powder cacurred on Thursday night at South Shields, in the house of John Pease, a miner. Mrs. Pease went with a light tc "molt for a screwdriver which her husband reqehed, when a spark fell upon 31ba. weight of blasting powder, which immediately exploded with dread- ful effect. Mrs. Pease and a girl named Geergina Hunter, aged 13, who was in the house, were shockingly burnt about the neck and face", besides sufiering a severe shock to the system. The housa was completely wrecked, the win- dows and ceiling being blown out. The windows of the adjoining houses were also broken. THU FEMALE 11IERSONATORS IN LITEPPOOL.—At the Liverpool city sessions, on Wednesday, Thomas Cole,. 21, ship's steward, and Robert Delaney, 22, waiter, both of whom have been brought up several times before the magis- trates and the Recorder for committing various robberies whilst the first-named prisoner was dressed in female clothes, were charged, Cole with having stolen a watch and chain from the person of George Jones (since deceased) on the 15th March law., and Delaney with having received the same knowing it to have been stolen. Cole was sentenced to five years' r;eenal servitude, and Delaney, against whom there were t';eo previous oenvietions, to seven ysArs' penal servittids,

div.head: _MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: _MISCELLANEOUS.

The Bishop of Bangor consecrated the English Church of St. Seiriol, at Pentnaenmarrr, on Saturday. rtimngova coeme.nt is on foot in Preston with the object of fo operative company for the regular supply of Cheap fish. The secretary of a Newcastle-on-Tyne building society 1,48 been sentenced to six months' imprisonment for em- oezzlement. It has been decided that none of the awards for the Pisheries Exhibition shall be announced till the date of the closing ceremony. The electric light, which has been provisional in the libraries and dining rooms of the House of Commons, will be Permanently instituted. The Bolton Corporation have erected a hospital for the treatment of cases of an infectious character, and the formal °Pening took place on Saturday. The Burnley magistrates have refused to renew fifty, or nearly one-third, of the "off " or grocers' licenses in that tOwe.rl, to the whole of which the police had objected. , AOlrew WALES COLLEGE.—Bangor has been unanimously elected by Lord Carlingfoed, Lord Bramwell, and Mr. Mun- della as the best site for the proposed college for North Wales. The first of the refrigerator cars sent for fish to Scotland by the Fish League, Limited, arrived in London on Mon- laY morning witle §0 baskets of herrings, which were sold at Colombia market, , rural letter tatri'ar having been arrested for fraudu- lently obtaining money for parcels sent by the Parcels Post, "° Postmaster-General desires it to be made known that all Payments for parcels are to be made by the senders. EDINGBURGII UNIVEIcSITY BUILDINGS COMPLETION fneete—Mr. Carnegie, of New York and Pittsburg, well "own for his munificent gifts to Dunfermline, his native city, has intimated a subscription of £l,OOO to this fund. ROBBERY BY A CORPORAL.—A corporal in the Royal Welsh Fusiliers named Gooding was on Monday sentenced to nine months' imprisonment for stealing various sums of tnoney belonging to other Solditrs stationed at Wrexham barracks. , ATTEetterap WIFE Willem—Joseph Drake, a retired olacksmith, 72 years of age, of Armley, Leeds, is in custody Charged with attempting to murder his wife. The crime Was a most determined one, the prisoner having hacked the Woman's throat dreadfully:with a razor. Mrs. Drake is in a Precarious state. TEE CHARGE OF EMBEZZLEMENT BY A SALESMAN.—At Liverpool, on Saturday, a mideqe-aged man, named James leeney, was committed for trial charged with having em- bezzled £4OO, the moneys of his employer, Samuel Vestey, Provision merchant, Mathew-street, Liverpool, whilst he was let Barbadoes. SHOCKING FATALITY TO A BOY.—A boy, aged twelve, named Frederick Scott, met with a horrible death at Shef- field, on Saturday. Whilst climbing an oak tree the bough ?Isl which he stood broke, and he fell upon some iron rail- tugs, one of which entered his stomach, causing death almost Instantaneously. A SALVATIONIST SENT TO PRISON. At Penzance, on Monday Frederick Chaplain, a captain in the Salvation Army, was fined 108. and costs for obstructing the thorough- fare by holding a service in one of t the principal streets of the borough. He refused to pay a fine, and was committed te gaol for 14 days. DRIVING THROUGH A REGIMENT.—A Preston tramcar driver was, on Monday, fined for forcing his horses and car Into the ranks of a Militia regiment which was marching through the streets of that town. He was warned to stop by the commanding officer, but drove on and scattered the men composing the column. ROUND THE WORLD IN EIGHTY-SIX DAYS —The New Zealand Shipping Company's steamer lonic has arrived at London from New Zealand. The lonic is the first large steamship which has passed through the Straits of Magellan, and on this her first voyage has made the passage round the world in 86 days under steam. TEE TWENTY-MILES BICYCLE CHAMPIONSHIP.—Over 10,000 persons were present at the Belgrave-road Grounds, Leicester, on Saturday, to witness the third race for the 20- mlle bicycle championship of the world, with belt value £5O and £25 added money. Wood, of Leicester, the present bolder, won, gaining the belt absolutely. CHILD MURDER.—We reported last week that a Staly- bridge trader, bringing home some parcels from Man- chester, found that one had been slipped in which contained tU's dead boely of a child. At the inquest the medical evi- dence went to show that death had arisen from suffocation, and a verdict of wilful murder was returned against some unknown person. DESTRUCTION or FISHING NETS. The fishing boats Which arrived at Peterhead, on Monday, reported an unpre- cedented destruction of fishing nets through the shoals of herrings king so dense. Very few boats had escaped with- out losing a portion of their nets, and many had lost the entire drift, the weight of the fish carrying them to the bot- tom of the sea. At some places off Berwick the sea seemed ksolid mass of herrings. • AN EXTRAORDINARY OUTRAGE is reported from the Rhondda Valley. A colliery which had been temporarily closed owing to wages disputes was entered during the night by some persons who destroyed the air-doors, pulled down the roof timbers, and placed a lighted candle in a remote working place. Ventilation being entirely suspended, an explosion occurred, but fortunately no one vies in the pip, and the damage was only slight. WRESTLING MATCH.—The most important match that as taken place near London for many years tookplace on Saturday afternoon at Saves Court, Deptford, betteeen John WannoP, of London, and Thomas Kennedy, of Egremont. Both are Cumberland and Westmoreland wrestlers. The match was open for £2OO, and they were to wrestle in the Cumberland. Devon, and L inceshire styles, one fall in each. The match terminated unsatisfactorily. THE LOCKERBIE RAIILWAY CALAMITY.—George Easton, the driver of the Stranraer train on the occasion of the fatal collision near Lockerbie on the Caledonian Railway, has been returned for trial at the Circuit Court of Justiciary, Dumfries, on a charge of culpable homicide, it being alleged that prisoner ran his train to the junction, notwith- standing that the signals were against him. Easton will be defended by the Amalgamated Society of Railway Ser- vants. TEE HOUSE OF COMMONS POSTOFFICE.—The weekly average of letters delivered to members from the postoffice ha the lobby of the House of Commons has been during the Pest session 22,698, and the weekly average of replies 13,000; 2,858 postal orders have been granted, and 959 money orders; 1,228 letters have been registered. and a sum of £2,843 received for stamps. Mere than half of the letters delivered at the Hons.e have to he redirected to members' Private addresses. TEE INCORPORATION OF BANGOI2..—The proclamation of Bangor as an incorporated city was made on Saturday, and was marked with demonstrations of a very extensive character. The day was observed as a holiday, and a large procession, including the volunteers, friendly societies, and boYs from the Clio training ship, marched to the square op- Posite the Masonic Hall, where, after certain formalities had been observed, the charter of incorporation was read by Mr. Re H. Pritchard, who is named therein as the first town clerk.

COLLISIONS AT SEA: Loss OF LIFE.—A collision occurred' oh Sunday morning between the Compagnie Generale's Transatlantic steamer St. German, from Havre for New York, and the steamer Woodburn, from the east, at a point 40 miles south-west of the Eddystone, resulting in the loss of the Woodburn, with 18 of her crew. The St. Germain Put into Plymeueh Sound disabled. The owners of the Woodburn have made a claim for £60,000 damages against the owners of the St. Germain. On Saturday afternoon the German steamer Palermo collided, off Umhant, an island on the north-west coast of France, with the steamer Rivoli, from Bilbao to Middlesborough. The Rivoli sank, carrying With her five of the crew. THE CONCLUSION OF THE SESSION.—An extraordinary scene was witnessed in the Reuse of Commons on Saturday. Half an hour after the Speaker had left the chair and the session was concluded an enormous crowd of persons had assembled outside the Houses of Parliament, and were ad- Initted through the Viekria Tower to view the Housa of Lords. After this they Rocked towards the House of Com- Mons in a steam that blocked all the lobbies, and the doors being opened, they filled the House itself. A rope had been dawn across the gangway by the table, and that part of the ouse was kept free from intrusion. Elsewhere the ,I,hamber was densely packed by a crowd, a little excited Y its unexpected privileges, but most orderly la de- meanour.

- SERIOUS FIRES —A. destructive fire broke out on Satur- day afternoon in Waln's certified warehouse, Lancelot's- hey. Liverpool, belonging to Messrs. Green and Taylor, vrhich was principally -stored with cotton, the property of several city merchants. The damage, which is covered by Insurance, is roughly eatimated at £2o,ooo.—At an early hour on Saturday morning fire was discovered in a truck attached to the Great Yorthern train from London to Man- -cheater. The train left 'King's Cross soon after ten, and When Grantham was reached the newspaper truck was found 14 be on tire. Before it could be extinguished over 6,000 -Papers and periodicals were destroyeel.—A fie, causing ,Slnage amounting to about £30,000, which is covered by inaurance, occurred on Sunday morning on the premises of Messrs. Henry Glover and Co., Limited, paper merchants, printers, dm., Hammerton-street, Bradford. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 1, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 1, 1883.
POLITICAL.

- In the last parliamentary paper for the session, issued on Tuesday, there kite 76 notices of motion for next session. Mr. Davenport Handley (L.) and Mr. Jas. W. Lowther (C) were on Monday nominated candidates for the representa- tion of the county of Rutland. The Hon. C. H. Strutt (Conservative) was on Saturday returned without opposition for East Essex, in the room of Colonel Ruggles-Brise, resigned. It is understood that Lord Randolph Churchill, who will return to London early next month, contemplates taking an active part in political life during the recess. At a meeting of the Fifeshire Constitutional Association, at Cupar, on Tuesday, Mr. Randolph Erskine Wemyss, whose father represented the county in the Liberal intetest, publicly joined the Conservative party. It was announced on Saturday that Mr. Jeune, the ac- cepted Conservative candidate for Lewes, bad found his professional engagements so great that he had been com- pelled to give up all idea of contesting the borough. The Observer says :—The impression is gaining ground that the Cabinet look forward to a dissolution of Parliament in the autumn of next year. The Ministerial programme for next Session will be specially framed with a view to this contingency. The select committee appointed to enquire into the con- dition and the position of the canals and internal naviga- tion of the country have reported the evidence already taken before them, and this has now been published in a bluebook of over 300 pages. The committee recommend their re-appointment next session. * No time will oe lost, the Observer states, in taking prac- tical steps to utilise the £50.000 voted for immigration pur- poses in Ireland. An association will forthwith be formed, comprising men of all shades of political opinion, with the object of furthering the scheme. An executive meeting of the Yorkshire Miners' Associa- tion, held at Barnsley, on Monday, recommended the adgp- tion of a resolution for the immediate formation of a pole- flea' association on the same lines as the one in operatter, in Durham with the object of returning one or more can- didates at ale next general election.

THE IRISH MAILS.—A deputation from the Dublin Chamber of Commerce on Wednesday waited on the Lord- Lieutenant seeking Government aid for a proposed line connecting the Dublin and Kingstown Railway with other railway systems, in order to facilitate the carriage of the mails inland and for the convenience of passengers. The Lord-Lieutenant could not promise that the Government would give a guarantee, but thought a loan at low interest might be given when a desirable scheme was formulated. :SINGULAR CASE OF BOYCOTTING.—An extensive trial of improved harvest machinerron view in the agricultural de- partment of Cork Exhibion was announced to take place on Thursday close to Blarney Castle. The farm selected for the contest was one from which the tenant has been evicted, and on this account boycotting noticos were postea up cautioning competitors of the consequences of their taking part in the trial. Owing to this the promoters had to abandon the affair.

THE IRISH NATIONAL LEAGIJE.-Mr. Parnell presided at a meeting of the Organising Committee of the Irish National League, held on Thursday in Dublin. Mr. Pavitt ales attended. The receipt of £2,011 was acknowledged since last meeting, and £550 was voted for the relief of evicted tenants in different parts:of the country. It is pro- posed to hold a series of great popular demonstrations throughout the provinces during the next fortnight. Mr. Parnell will address his constituents early in September. A BRAVE LADY.-At Cabra, a Dublin suburb, on Sunday evening, a burglar entered the house of Mr. Crolly, who with all his family, except his wife, was absent. The lady found the burglar under a sofa in the drawing-room. She at once locked the door, and went out for constable, but, meeting a man, she sent him for the police, and rettniied herself to the house, where she covered the 'burglar with a revolver, keeping him a prisoner until the police came. The burglar was on Monday sentenced to three months' hard labour.

EVICTION OF A PRIEST —Thq itev. ThOiiia9 Ferris, priest, was on Thursday eviclta 't)ye the sub-sberiff and a large military and police force from his residence and farm on the estate of Mr. John Parrott, of Castlelynns. He refused to pay rent for three years, demanding a reduction in respect of a house on his land built by a predecessor, for whose title he had paid a large sum of money. He suffered the eviction to prove his consistency as a Nationalist sym- pathiser. His furniture was placed in a hut erected in the graveyard attached to the parish church. DEATH OF A NOTORIOUS IRISH NATIONALIST. News has been received of the death, at Lourdes, of Mr. Daniel O'Sullivan, who as Mayor of Cork in 1868, created such a stir in the political world. Mr. O'Sullivan, during his tenure of office, was a pronounced Nationalist, and white presiding at a supper in Cork in honour of Messrs. Warren and Cos- tello, who had just been released from prison, referred in remarkable language to the attempted assassination of the Duke of Edinburgh. A special bill was introduced into Parliament to deprive him of his office of mayor, and he was summoned to the Bar of the House of Commons to answer for his conduct. On the advice of the late Mr. Maguire, M.P., he saved Mr. Gladstone's Ministry further trouble by voluntarily resigning the mayoralty. After that eventful period Mr. O'Sullivan lived in retirement. MR. PARNELL ON THE PAST .SESSlON.—Spealling at a meeting of the National League at Dublin, on Wednesday, Mr. Parnell urged the necessity of attending to registration, as the approaching revisions would in all probability decide the registry upon which issue would be taken at the next general election. In Parliament they had procured several most valuable measures in the interests of the Irish people. The Fisheries Act, the Labourers' Act, and the Tramways Act would be valuable only in a second degree to the Irish Land and Arrears Acts of 1881 and 1882. They Lad per- fected a plan of migration which, if successful, would give them an unanswerable argument for the application of further and larger sums next session in the same direction, and would bring about a redistribution of population in congested districts. He expressed his belief that the day was not far distant when they will have gained the fall pro- gramme of the National League. . THE CHARGE OF CONSPIRACY TO MURDER.—The In- quiry was resumed at Limerick on Saturday into the charges against Dr. Wm. P. Connolly, and his father, Thomas Connolly, of Bruff, for conspiring to murder John Carroll, and attempting to administer poison to Carroll and his sister.—The evidence of Michael Dineen was to the effect that about the beginning of January last, when in Connolly's house, he swore on a prayer book to "do away with" John Carroll. He west:, get fifty pounds for doing the job, and was to be "done away with" himself if he did not obey Connolly's order. The doctor gave witness a revolver the following night. The witness and Tom Con- nolly were to lie in ambush and shoot Carroll. The signal was to be given by the doctor. They lay in ambush several nights, but the plot did not succeed. The witness also stated that the doctor had arranged to put chloroform or vitriol on a handkerchief which the witness was to throw in Miss Carroll's face, but the witness refused. The examina- tion of Dineen had not concluded when the Court adjourned. Mr. Justice Murphy, sitting in Chambers on Tuesday, gave liberty in the case of Connolly v. Carroll to extend , the time to defend. The plaintiff is Dr. Connolly, Bruff, county Limerick, at present charged with conspiring to murder the defendant, who is bailiff on a local estate, and the action is for slander, damages being laid for £2,000. The words complained of are that Dr. Connolly had conspired to murder Carroll.

He had reason to believe it was out of sympathy for her and the family of the late Mr. Jenks that she had been allowed to remain at the Fox Inn; and if the firm under whom she held the house could see their way to transfer her to a house that was not frequented by such rough characters as went to the Fox Inn, and who could never be turned out until the house was pulled down, he should be glad.— Councillor Monks: It is not that Mrs. Jenks knowingly and willingly permits these characters to frequent the house?— The Clerk: A woman is not able to manage it.—The Chief Constable: Some women would manage it better than _ _ _ _ _ _

many men, but Mrs. Jenks has not nerve- and confidence sufficient.—Major Cartwright: The fact is such characters as the chief constable speaks of go in perhaps half a dozen at once, get something to drink, and then they create a die- turbance, a fight takes place or something of that sort, and an officer has to be sent for. I quite agree with the chief constable that they are some of the worst characters in War- . _

rington ; and from what he has said this morning I fancy they almost set him at defiance.—The Chief Constable : Certainly, and two or three police officers they set at de- fiance.—Major Cartwright: And if you can't manage them it is quite impossible for Mrs. Jenks to do so.—Mr. E irk- connel (Messrs. Davies, Sharp, and Kirkconnel) said the house belonged to Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., who always endeavoured to get respectable tenants, and be had no doubt the company would act upon Mr. Hunt's sugges- tion regarding Mrs. Jenks. She was under notice to quit, which expired in November, but she had been permitted to remain there for the sake of her family.—He thought if she had another chance she would do better.—The considera- tion of this application was deferred.

div.head: PERSONAL.
div.p: PERSONAL.

The Queen arrived at Balmoral on Saturday. incess Louise has presented a bust of herself at the age of three years to the Canadian National Art Gallery. The London Gazette announces the appointment of the Marquis of Lansdowne as Governor-General of Canada. The Marquis of Hartington has promised to be present at the feast of the Master Cutler at Sheffield, to be held on the 6th of next month. _ _

The Earl of Leicester, as president, has just added to the permanent fund of the Norfolk and Norwich Hospital the princely donation of £15,000. Mr. Gladstone contributes to the forthcoming number of the Nineteenth Century a translation into Italian of Cowper's well-known hymn, " Hark, my soul, it is the Lord." Mr. Gladstone arrived at Hawarden tlom London on Saturday evening. On Sunday morning the right hon. gentleman attended service at Hawarden Church, and read the lessons. Signor Fontana has executed three full-sized statues in Carrara marble of the Queen, the Prince of Wales, and of an allegorical figure representing New South Wales, for the new Government offices at Sydney. Her Majesty the Queen has presented Mr. Edwd Temple, Overleigh,Lode, Chester, late of the Scots' Fusilier Guards, with a copy of a photograph of himself, taken on the return of the Guards from the Crimea, in 1856. Lord Coleridge attended the services at Trinity Church, ' New York, on Sunday morning, occupying Mr. John Jacob Astot's pew. In the afternoon the Lord Chief Justice and his son were the guests of Judge Kapallo at the Manhattan, Coney Island. A singular honour has been conferred on the Marquis of Lorne. He has been elevated to the position of chief of an Indian tribe, with a high-sounding title from the red men's point of view, though not particularly acceptable to ears polite on this side of the Atlantic. The Marquis is to be formally installed at Quebec as Kondearente or the rat of the Lorette tribe,. the Princess Louise is to take part in the cere- mony. Major-General Sir Evelyn Wood, G.C.M.M. and ,V.C., was among the passengers who arrived at Plymouth on Sun- day night by the Peninsular and Oriental Company's steamer Indus. A large party of General Wood's friends were present. The general, though in excellent spirits, ap- peared to have suffered from his Egyptian experiences. His arrival was on the amiversary of his return from his exploits in Zululand exactly four years ago.
IRELAND. It is reported that Mr. Parnell will contest County Down at the next election on Home Rule principles.

div.head: ANNUAL BREWSTER SESSIONS.
div.p: ANNUAL BREWSTER SESSIONS.
WARRINGTON.

The annual Brewster Sessions for the borough of War- rington were held on Tuesday, at the Borough Police Court, the magistrates present being—Major Cartvright (who pre- sided), Alderman Webster, Alderman Chandley, and Coun- cillor Monks. THE CHIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT.

The Chief Constable presented his annual report, which I showed that there were in the town 87 licensed victuallers, I 48 beerhouse-keepers, and 77 shopkeepers, SZ3.. there being ' a fallieg off in the latter of 9 as compared with the previous ! year. During the year six liceosed victuallers had been proceeded against, four of whom were convicted, and two ! dismissed; live beerhouse-keepers had been summoned and all of them convicted; and one shopkeeper had been sum- ' moned, but the case was dismissed. Of 717 persons charged with drunkenness, 617 were convicted, and 100 dismissed. , The following table shows the number of persons charged ' with drunkenness during the past 10 years : Convicted. There were three applications for transfers of licenses, and an application for victuallers' license by an off license holder.

div.p: TIIANSFF.RS.

The transfers were as follow :—Gardeners' Arms, Brick- street. from Thomas Taylor to Richard Bice, granted ; Stamford Arms, Stamford-street, from Ann Woodall to Peter Woodall, granted; and off license for 109, Winwick•road, from John H. Sherlock to Samuel Fulwood, adjourned.

div.p: TIIE BLACK LIST.

The Clerk said last year the rule was adopted of stating that the licenses were renewed except such as were objected to without reading over the long list of n'ames.—Conucillor Monks: Are there any exceptions ?—The Clerk (to Mr. Hunt) : What licenses are there yon have given notice of objection to ?—The Chief Constable : Those of Henry Git- tens, Jane Jenks, Charles Roddy, Ann Bailey, and John Foy.

div.head: TURF-LOVING LANDLORD.
div.p: A TURF-LOVING LANDLORD.

Henry Gittens, who was convicted of refusing to admit the police, and fined 40s. and costs, and had his license en- dorsed, on the 27th October last year, was then called before the Bench.—The Chief Constable said he felt it his duty to inform their worships that the applicant before them was a betting man and a bookmaker, and that he had persons of that class visiting his house. He (Mr. Hunt) had received reports of their transactions over and over again, not only from the police but from other persons, and he felt it his duty, knowing G Wens to be a young man of previous good character—he had been in the employ of Walker and Son for years, and was well conducted—to go out of his way to call upon him and tell him of the reports he had received. Gitteus remarked that it was strange such reports should be made, but he (the Chief Constable) was convinced he was right, and he must tell the Bench that notwithstanding his caution he had every reason to believe that that sort of thing was going on.—Major Cartwright: Even now ?—The Chief Constable: Well, I have not heard anything this last month or two; but I know his propensity for horse racing, betting, and so forth, which is contrary to law, and I feel it my duty to suppress that as much as I possibly can, and I shall never hesitate to let the magistrates know of a person of that sort holding a license.—Mr. Gittens said he was very sorry the case had occurred, and he would take care the like did not occur again. As to betting since the conviction, such had not been the case.—The Chief Constable said a betting club had corn- ntenced in Orford-street, and at the head of it was a publi- can. It was doing a great deal of damage to the young men of the town, there was no doubt of that.—Major Cart- wright asked if the-Chief Constable had any confidence in the applicant as to the future.—The Chief Constable: It is just possible a remonstrance from you this morning might suffice.—Councilior Monks: Have you ever fonnd remon- strances to do any good ?—Major Cartwright: Yes; I know of several cases.—The Chief Constable said it had been the custom to adjourn the consideration of these licenses until the transfer day, when the magistrates granted them; but he did not see any good in it.—The Clerk • It has only been a farce, because when the day has come the lieenees have been granted.—Major Cartwright: The case must stand over for a moment or two.

div.head: NOT SUFFICIENT NERVE.
div.p: NOT SUFFICIENT NERVE.

Mrs. Jane Jenks, of the Fox Inn, Buttermarket-street, who was convicted on the 18th December last year for per- mitting disorderly conduct, and fined 103. and costs, next applied for the renewal of her license.—Mr. Hunt said the applicant had held a license since the 2nd of October last year, her husband having died in June or July previously. Mrs. Jenks was a respectable, industrious womau, and had been left with a large family of young children. Her house however, was frequented by a very low lot of people —in fact the worst class of people in the town, and he was very sorry to say it respecting anybody, and especially against a woman like Mrs. Jenks, but she certainly was not

At Birkenhead, on Tuesday, the soi-disant Champion Penman of the World, who stood charged with obtaining money by fraudulent pretences, was committed for trial. HEAVY FAILURE.—The suspension is announced of Messrs. Richards, Power, and Co., steamship owners, mer- chants, and smelters, Swansea and London,; the liabilities being estimated at about £350,000. A COMMUTED DEATH SENTENCE.—At the recent Swansea asezes, Lieorge Isaac Knight was sentenced to death for the wilful murder of his wife in the Rhondda Valley. 'lbis sentence has now been commuted to penal servitude for

life. FATAL FOOTBALL ACCIDENT.—James Gordon, a football player, died in Arbroath on Tuesday from the effects of an injury accidentally caused when playing in a match last Saturday between the Arbroath Club and the South-western of Glasgow Club. A NAVAL LrEirrENANT DlSMlSSED.—Lieutenant Storey, who was navigating Her Majesty's ship Eclipse when she came into collision with a merchanttnan recently, was, on Wednesday, dismissed his ship, and ordered to forfeit all

seniority as lieutenant. UNWHOLESOME SAllSAGES.—David:Grahatn, wholesale and retail bu'cher, in New City-road, Glas9zow, was on Tuesday fined £5, with the alternative of 40 days' imprisonment, for selling sausages unfit for food. The sausages had been seasoned or freshened in colour with sulphate of lime. The POSTMASTER-GENERAL, it if; stated, has consented to allow light packets of medicine to be conveyed by carriers in the country, provided that there is no intprference with the due performance of the mail service; but it is intimated that in the event ef the privilege being abused it will be

withdrawn. FALL OF HOUSES.—On Monday ten houses in Garrie- street, Boosbeck, gave way. and the inmates had the greatest difficulty in getting their goods out. The post office building has been condemned by the suiveyor as unfit for habitation. Several families had to camp out on

Sunday night. A SWIM ACROSS THE SOLENT.—Mr. George White, of the Portsmouth Swimming Club, swam across the Solent on Monday morning in two hours and fifty-two minutes. Mr. Evans, the well-known swimmer, also tried, but failed. Captain Webb was once unsuccessful in attempting to ac- complish this feat. CHILD MURDER BY A MOTHEE.—At Cierkenwell Police Court, on Wednesday, Johanna Culverwell, 27, married woman, of Mason's-place, St. Luke's, was remanded, charged on her own confession with wilfully murdering her male child, aged five weeks, by drowning him in a pan of water on Tuesday evening. ATTEMPTED MURDER OF A FATHER.—At Birmingham, on Wednesday, a man named John Corley was attacked by his son, a man 30 years of age, who had returned drunk from Warwick races, and on being remonstrated with for turning out the contents of a box in the bedroom, beat his father with a huge stick until he was insensible. ALLEGED FRAUDULENT BANICRUPTCY.—A Birmingham draper named James Jones was on Tuesday committed for trial charged with fraudulent bankruptcy. The defendant failed for £15,000, with but trifling assets; and it is alleged that he had previously sold under heavy discounts large quantities of goods bought in Manchester and Bradford. DEPARTURE OF MORMONS.—On Wednesday the Guinn steamer Nevada sailed from the Mersey for New York, having on board 659 Mormons, who are on their way to Salt Lake City. Of the number 284 are Scandinavians, 106 Germans and 269 British. The British include people from England, Scotland, and Wales, but none from Ireland. JEWELLERY ROBBERY.—Cbief Constable Ferndale of Birmingham, on Tuesday, received a consignment of dam- aged jewellery which has since been identified as part of the stock stolen from Messrs. Mole and Sons, High-street, Bir- , minghant and valued at over £5,000. The articles had been found in a parcel in the River Mersey during some

dredging operations. RDE a AND ATTEMPTED MIT BD EEL—The Ipswich magistrates on Monday committed Thomas Lyms Day, a moulder, for trial at the nest assizes. on the charge of wil- fully murdering a little girl, four years old, his illegitimate daughter, by cutting her throat. The prisoner was also committed for trial on the charge of attempting to murder

the child's stepfather. A SROCANG SUICIDE took place on Tuesday, at Birming- ham Barracks, where a troop of the nth Hussars are new stationed. Private Lambert went into his room smoking a cigar, and, without giving any indication of what he was about to do, discharged his carbine into his mouth. He pulled the trigger with the spar on his boot. The discharge almost blew the man's head to pieces. FATAL QUARREL AMONGST WOMEN. - A fatal quarrel between women occurred at Glasgow on Monday. Four females who were drinking together had a dispute, and three of them, aged respectively 19,21, and 23, attacked the wife of a shoemaker named Murray, of Naburn-street, South- side. They knocked her down, beating and kicking her to such an extent that her death resulted half an hour after-

The next applicant was Charles Roddy, of the Bull's Head, Bridge-street, who was convicted in Jane this year for permitting disorderly condct, and fined 5s and costs. Roddy was also convicted in 1877 for permitting drunken- ness, and fined 40s and costs.—Mr. Hunt thought it his duty to inform the magistrates that Roddy had a christen- ipg on the Sunday, and he had invited his friends from Cheshire to celebrate the event, but he put too much rum in their tea, and they got fighting %Ith each other. (Laughter.) —Major Cartwright: They were too merry.—The Chief Constable: His wife had had twins. (Laughter.)—Coun- cillor Monks: That accounts for it! (Laughter.)—Mr. , Kirkconnel called the attention of the Bench to the fact that the first conviction took place six years ago, and be thought the last case was a very slight one indeed.—Major Cart- wright: Yes, I recollect it very well indeed. I suppose if there is a complaint against any holder of a licence under your company you immediately give the person notice Mr. Kirkconnel : Not necessarily that they must go, but if the Bench think it proper they should go, they do so.— Councillor Monks: Your action depends upon the magis- trates ?—Mr. Kirkconnel : Of course.
The Bench then retired, and after about quarter of an hour's absence returned into court.

Major Cartwright said Gittens's was the most serious case the magistrates had had before them, but in consequence of what the chief constable had said in his favour the Bench had decided to grant his application. However, he must bear in mind that the license was granted for another 12 months on the understanding that he closed his house against all betting transactions and betting men. That alone would save him in the future, and fairly conducting his house. It was by no means by the unanimous decision of the Bench that he got his license granted, but it was on the distinct understanding he bad stated that it was granted. The con- viction would be brought against him and he would be sure to have his license taken from him if he did not con- duct himself properly. The license was granted this time. As to Mrs. Jenks, the magistrates felt that she was hardly able to conduct a house of the description of the Fox Inn, and if the firm she was now living under could find her an- other house more suitable for her management the Bench themselves would be glad for her sake, she having been left in the manner described by Mr. Hunt. That would be a matter for her and the company to deal with hereafter; meanwhile the magistrates granted the license. He advised Mrs. Jenks not to supply these characters with drink. It was very hard to shut customers out, but if they would not ' conduct themselves properly, and cease giving her and the Inonce trouble, it was the only course to be pursued.—Mr. police (on behalf of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co.) said after what the Bench had said he would try to find IMrs. Jenks another house.—Coming to Roddy's case, Major Cartwright asked if the honse had not been condacted I well since that particular Sunday.—The Chief Constable: Yes.—Major Cartwright said the magistrates felt inclined to grant Roddy his license on the understanding that he conducted his house as well as he possibly could. They knew it was a rough neighbourhood on Saturday and Sunday I nights, and he had his Home renewed on that understand- ling.—Councillor Monks: Next time you have a christening don't put so much rum in the tea. (Laughter.) DRUNKENNESS AMONGST WOMEN: STARTLING STATEMENTS. _ _

The Clerk said themwere five convictions against beer- house keepers, but the -houses had changed hands, with the exception of the White Bear, in Buttermarket-street. This house was kept by John Foy, who had been fined 20s and costs for permitting drunkenness.—Mr. Hunt said he had had no complaints latterly respecting this house' and he was hopeful of it being conducted better. He, however. ' called attention to the fact that this house was very much frequented by young girls in their teens.—Major Cart- wright: What, now ?—The Chief Constable: Yes, and ever since he has kept it.—Major Cartwright: Are they fustian . cutters?—The Chief Constable: Factory hands and young girls of all descriptions. He did not wish to name any particular class. They commenced going into public-houses at 14 years of age, and went on from that age upwards. There were more drunken women in town now than he thought Warrington ever had before. Especi- ally was drunkenness prevalent amongst young girls. Two or three of them went into public-houses for a quart of beer, and if they had not got money to pay for it they took off their shoes, or skirt, to raise the money.—Major Cart- , , wright : Is he cognisant of the fact ?—The Chief Constable: ; He is cognisant of the fact that his house is frequented by , young girls. Warrington wAs becoming famous for young ;girls drinking.—Major Cartwright: A landlord can refuse to fill for girls ?—The Clerk: There is a general discretion. A landlord has no legal right to refuse to supply drink un- less there is a reneon for it.—Councillor Monks : It is reasonable to refuse to serve a girl of 14.—The Chief Constable: I • went into Foy's house one Sunday 1 and counted 40 or 50 young girls 'all round the room.—Mr. Foy said four of the party were going to America, and that was the reason they were in his house. There had been nothing of the sort since.—The Chief Con- ' stable : I am sorry to say that we have two or three young girls, 14 or 15 years of age, that we look upon as young prostitutes and drunkards.—Mr. Foy: We don't allow cha- Iracters of that sort in our house.—The Chief Constable: It is just the place where we have found them.—Mr. Kirk- Iconnel observed that with the exception of allowing these Iyoung girls to assemble, there was nothing against the house.—The Chief Constable said Foy had been convicted , several times, and was a hard learner. He hoped his re- I marks would have effect; he would be sorry to see Foy lose his license.—Major Cartwright: Will your promise to stop this sort of thing P—Foy : I will, your worship.— Major Cartwright: If you don't the Chief Constable will have his eye upon you; but on the understanding we have come to the Bench grant the license.—Mr. Kirkconnel said Foy was under notice, and if this conduct was con- tinued the notice would be enforced. • DARESBURY. The annual Brewster Sessions for Daresbury were herd at the Sessions House, Dareabury, on Tuesday, before Mr. Edward Greenall and Mr. H. Pierpoint. From Superin- tendent Williamson's report it appeared that in the district there were 23 licensed victuallers, two beer sellers, and three others who sold off the premises, making a total of 28, which gave an average of 299 of the population to each license. Two licensed victuallera had been proceeded against daring the year, both being convicted. One beerseller had been proceeded against, but the case was dismissed. During the year 35 persons had been convicted of drunkenness, showing an increase of six over those of last year. The popalation was 8,361. Thomas Hindley, Cat and Lion, Stretton, for permitting drunkenness on Oct. 30th last year, had been fined 40s and costs; Joseph Miller Mulberry Tree, Appleton, for a similar offence, on May Miller, this year, had been fined 20s and costs; and William Worrell, Whitley, tor allowing in- toxicating drir;ks to be consumed on his premises, on August 19th last year, was refused a certificate at the adjourned licensing meeting in September last. All the licenses were renewed except in the cases where convictions had been obtained, and in the case of Peter Joynson, these being al journed until September 25th.—Superintendent Williamson stated in reference to the case of Peter Joynson than he was led to belreve he had allowed drunkenness on his premises.

NEWTON. The annual session fOr the renewal and granting of licenses for the ensuing year was held at Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, the magistrates on the Bench being George McCorquodale, R. Houghton, C. Pilkington, and A. C McCorquodale, Efqs.—Superintendent Jackson (of Leigh) presented his annual report in connection with the Warrington County Police Division, which showed that there were 43 licensed victuallers; and during the year ending 31st July last there were 3 conviction'; previous year, 1. Beerhouse-keepers, 15 ; convictions last year, 0; previous year, 4. There were 11 off-license holders, none of whom were convicted; there was one application for a billiard and bagatelle license, and two applications for the rehewal of sweets, wines, and grocers' licenses. The summary, sh •wed that the population was 21,510; the number of town- ships, 12; licensed victuallers, 47; beerhouses, 15 ; outdoor licenses, 11; convictions during 1883, 3 ; previous year, 5. In 1883, 162 persons were summoned for drunkenness, and 179 in 1882; decrease 17. Tke number apprehended was as follows :-1883, 66 • 1882, 54; increase 12. Superin- tendent Weir's report of tke Wigan division showed that the number of licensed victuallers was 12; proceeded against 0; spirit-grocers, 2; proceeded against, 0; beerhouses, 14; proceeded against, 2; off-license holders, 5. In 1883 41 persons were apprehended and 270 were summoned for all kinds of offences; while in the previous year 41 were ap- trehended and 266 summoned.—The Deputy Clerk (Mr. White) stated that there were no objections to any renewals of licenses, and they would all be granted to the applicants in an adjoining room.—This was the whole of the business in connection with the Licensing Sessions.

AI2GE OF SHOOTING A WIFE.—John Sparks, an inn- keeper. was remanded by the Hereford m4giatrates, on Thursday, on the charge of shooting his wife, who is dangerously wounded. The affair was at first supposed to be accidental.

Three men were on Thursday thrown out of a carriage while descending the Penrhewfer Colliery, Rhondda Valley. Their dead bodies were found at the bottom. THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL Maim—There was on Tuesday a quiet market, and generally throughout the iron trade of this district there is an absence of animation. The business doing in pig iron is extremely small, buyers preferring to wait rather than purchase forward. The better class makers are under no actual necessity to offer induce- ments in the shape of reduced prices, but there are some in- ferior district brands to be bought at low figures. Lanca- shire makers hold firmly for 455. to 455. 6d. less 2 for forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to Manchester, and are indifferent about booking orders. In district brands, although the slight upward tendency which was noticeable a week or two back has scarcely been maintained, 443. 103. to 455. 10d. less for forge and foundry Lincoln- shire delivered here remains about the minimum basis for good brands. Finished iron makers have as a rule their books full of orders for the present, and there is a steady influx of work. Prices for delivery into the Manchester district are steady at £6 2s. 6d. to £6 ss. for ordinary bars £6 10s. to £6 12s. 6d. for hoops, and £8 ss. to £8 7s. 6d for sheets. The shipping trrde is showing more animation, and American buyers are beginning to make inquiries in the market.—As intimated last week the present month is closing with a pretty general advance in the price of round coal, and in anticipation of this upward movement there has naturally been an extra pressure of demand. This, however, has not been to any very large extent, and it cannot be said that there is any actually great pressure for supplies generally. Pits are kept running pretty nearly full time, but there is a more than sufficient output to meet present requirements, and the upward movement, is rather in anticipation of the rush of orders which have come forward during the autumn of the two previous years than an advance based upon any present largely increased demand. There is, however, for house fire coals a more active inquiry than is usual at this time of the year; common round coals are also moving off freely for shipment, and upon these two classes of coal ad- vances of from 6d to is per ton are being put in force gene- rally at the pits throughout West Lancashire, whilst the leading firms in the Manchester district are putting 10,1 on to their delivered rates for house fire coals. For next month hest coal is now quoted at 10s, seconds at Bs, and common round coals at Os to 6s 6d per ton at the pits, and the advance is also being followed in quotations for ship- ment, although not to the same extent. Other classes of fuel are without change, burgy and slack still meeting with only a slow sale at late rates, and for these pit prices remain at about 4s 6d to 5s for burgy, 3s 6cl to 4s for good slack, and 3s to as 3{l for common sorts,

div.p: THE EXAMINER..
SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 1, 1883.

MR. BRIGHT'S speech on the, licensing question, delivered at Birmingham on Wed" nesdAy, will, from the peculiar attitude the right hon. gentleman has always assumed towards this subject, be read with mtle? interest, by his political friends, and by 11,15 political opponents as well. Mr. BRIGHT S deliverance comes at a very opportune moment, when the annual licensing meeting! are being held throughout the country, ana when probably at this more than at any other time the necessity for the control of the drink traffic being placed in the hands of a bodY responsible to public opinion is more than ever apparent. Mr. BRIGHT never has been a supporter of the principle of the Permissive, Bill; still he is not less sincere than some ?' the extreme advocates of that measure denouncing the present licensing system, ana urging the necessity for its reform. He would) however, prcceed cautiously—step by step' and he would recognise vested interests. Ile use his own words, "If a trade in this country is permitted by law, that trade has a right to be defended by law ; " and again, 'O long as it (the trade) is not condemned b 7 Parliament, it has a right to demand that it should not be subjected to passionate ana hasty legislation." On the other hand, the friends of the Permissive Bill have no CO sideration whatever for the interests of the thousands of people who have invested their capital in public-houses. Because the trade is to them distasteful, they would place it in the power of the majority in a cool: munity to entirely sweep it away without. offering any compensation to the publicans and licensed victuallers. By so doing theY would also deprive a very considerable minority of what is considered by them 3 source of recreation and enjoyment. The bill was altogether too sweeping in its char', acter, it would certainly have prove tyrannical in its opefation, and therefore found comparatively little favour. Some °., its adherents were very lukewarm in the,ll support; because, indeed, they felt it woo" have been an injustice to have passed Such. bill.
