"points out, Lorpu,,,,z-". are entrusted with the power of providing us with gdz Paying our streets, making our sewers, con- trolling the police, and attending to sanitary 'natters, and that being so, it is surely not un- -reasonable that Corporations should also be entrusted with the granting and withholding licenses under certain limitations. These lirnitations Mr. BRIGHT has specified. • In the first place he says he would not allow any Corporation in the kingdom to increase the "Ilunlber of licenses at present granted. He assumes the number now sufficient for the Wants of the population, and would not per- -4t any increase; the propriety of increasing chinking facilities with the increase of the PoPulation is another matter. Then he would establish another limit, namely, that it should not be in the power of a Corporation—or anY committee to whom the licensing question Illight be relegated—to reduce the number eflicenses where the population remains the ..sarne to a degree less than one-half. He 1:°11.1d do this because he thinks that in Igislating in a matter of this kind violent ,e,l'anges are not necessary and not wise; and "80 because it is not right to create alarm, and to encourage that deprecation of pro- -1144' which would take place were it believed "Lat a Corporation would at once or in a tsuort time suppi ess all public-houses within ;Ile limits of their authority Further, Mr. ~,axGRT would at first confine the operation ' such a bill to boroughs only, and limit its e,xistence to ten years. If the experiment t'arned out a success then he would extend it a°_, Counties, and adapt its provisions to the ifanced state of temperance opinion. The es paid to the Government by all the rulic-houses and sellers of alcohol Mr, „ItIGHT would hand over to the Chancellor Of the Exchequer of each Corporation, who ilithight employ it in relieving the pressure of 'le education rate, for the purpose of re- ttril"ing a portion of the local taxes, in estroyincrb a class of houses in certain 4,eighbourhoods which are injurious '`elld far too numerous, and in providing °lllPensation for owners and occu- piers. Such is Mr. BRIGHT'S scheme, 4ad we venture to think it will corn- itself as being wise and statesmanlike. Possesses one great advantage in that it b."?uld obviate the election of special boards, "Ilich would of necessity be composed of tiersons of extreme views in favour either of ti7al abolition of the drink traffic or of some- akin to a free trade policy therein. Mr. t4),atGßT's scheme is a mild one compared with remedy of Sir WILFRID LAWSON and his :lends. Their's is one of confiscation and termination; Mr. BRIGHT'S is based on hquitY and justice, and in addition to that it ractically places the whole question in the i•entrol of the ratepayers, who can make their lifillence felt at each recurring municipal election.

11141 t. P. SPEARMAN AND THE BEASLEY BILL.—At the next eeting of the Rurc im Board of Commissioners Mr. P. Peakman will move that a coremittee be appointed to in- rthire into the Beasley Bill. th":47Elli.oo BRIDGE, RUNCORN.—About four months ago h• oard of Commissioners decided that Waterloo Bridge ould , widene I, a footway made for passengers, and other l'lnVeraents effected. Weak-minded men are very facile forrnin_ h g resolutions, but lack the strength of will and the ItlvivacirY to carry them out. Our local Authority seems to %e'er under a somewhat similar disadvantage. Although lit°ne3' required to improve the bridge was borrowed "'lra a th„ gn, it still lies rusting in the coffers of the Board, and 4 structure remains in its dangerous and disgraceful state, t Inenace to foot-passengers through its narrowness and un- ;et. surface. When traversing its length there must be no tioe'°ecupation—the mind must not be lost in the considera- lt 11 01 abstract questions of thought. Quick eyes and wary Cl'eTaents are required to avoid the luffibering !miry or dodge tile 1' tghter vehicle, the cab, as they travel to and from the :11way station ; awl persons of nervous disposition almost wettable with fear when, rubbing shoulders against the bridge they gaze upwards at a heavily laden cart, which ap- l'earsabout to topple over and crush them beneath its weight, Itlllle feet are drawn from the track ot the wheels with a ue°l33lll.sive movement, in dread of crushed toes or sprained ;1,11". Autumn is here, and soon wmter with its rain and *ll SS. will make the best formed road an unpleasant :eh's, will be upon us, and if the alterations are not in the „413 While carried out at Waterloo Bridge, the main ti‘aorongLfare to the railway station will,as was the case many ttleo last winter, be an almost imp issahle stream of water %be Mud. A question to the chairman of the Highway Com- tee at the Board meeting on Wednesday next will, per- set the municipal machine rolling in the desired rectiofi RrNCORI'T COMMISSIONERS' ELECTION.—The annual tio'"tietl of five members on the Runcorn Board of Commis. nen takes place on Thursday next, when the ratepayers Witt lave an opportunity of recording by their votes their iia):lll°n on some of the events of the past two years. So lit the contest seems to be exciting but little interest, no t eratere of any description his been issued, and the only 44404/411da. tes announced are those selected by the Ratepayers' Ilation—Mr. F. Fairhurst and Mr. Henry White. But „ "43' be the calm, whice, it is said, always precedes a liset;111, and the day of election may see some of those lively tst;ilea which have characterised it in days gone by. The *lilting members are Dr. Steele, Dr. MacDougall, Messrs. U. Shaw, and P. Speakman. Mr. Rhodes, we re• to say, has determined not to offer himself for re-elec- "' and the town will lose the services of a faithful re- abseaelltative, who without ostentatiously parading his views it"cl Opinions, has furthered the interests of the community 0,•-„eve5Y possible way It is rumoured, too, that Dr. Steele ta.'llria to retire from any public participation in local ti4ittero connected with the Board of Commissioners, but 4,4 requires conirmation, and .is an improbable con- e ZilnY• Speculation is rife as to the names which will , the " Works " list, but observing their usual secrecy, e 'Works," are not likely to show their " hand " until the 44;706 ,°f the election. One question frequently asked is 111 Dr. MacDougall have a place?" and it cannot now eoct°lowered with any degree of certainty. The worthy „ himself is apparently supremely indifferent on the I'9ect, and whilst the town will be in the throes of a con- Which he has often played a prominent part in past tile°, he will be far away amid the bracing breezes and tht!gged hills of bonnie Scotland with a newly made bride by 11111111de. Mr. R. Shaw and Mr. P. Speakman held seats on 2 Board as the nominees of the "Works," and there is no .°41104 to doubt that they will again have the aid of that Pew erful organisation. It is sincerely to be hoped that no contretemps as that which occurred at the last election be."ril take place on the present occasion. It will be remem- m,.l4 that last year the poll was closed a little over an hour tlfe aPening no vote having been recorded during that We believe, however, that the Ratepayers' Associa- ":" made provision against so impotent a conclusion t. She was bahrged with stealing a pair of boots, value 3s. 9d., ds3,-",gl,_ng to Noah Batley, of Cooper-street.—On Wedues- of ‘°s 22nd August, the prisoner was visiting at the house Iteroeac.c'ek and after her &parcure the apron and petticoat tet4 tnimed. THE Comma K—.—Cammack.—.Adyt. Swine fever has appeared on the premises of Mrs. Alice qui Mr. James Kearns, Widnes. m feverr. James e sa plipeeaarrnesd, on'twheillprenrais'es—of. of Widnee. PIC-NIC FROM WlDNES.—Tvgenty members of the Widnes Parish Church Bible Class had their annual pie-me to Chester, on Wednesday, and under the guidance of Mr. F. H. Pankhurst, the president, they spent a pleasant time in the ancient city. Tim MARQUIS OF CHoLmoNDELEy, accompanied by several ladies and his local agent, Mr. Henry Beswick, of Barrow Hall, visited Runcorn on Tuesday, and inspected his property on Runcorn Hill, afterwards driving to Halton Castle, and thence to Frodsham. HELSBY HILL SKETCHED BY A RUNCORN ARTIST.— Mr. J. Beesley, of High-street, is exhibiting in his window an oil painting of Helsbv Hill and the landscape beyond, the view being taken from Dunsdale Hollow. It is a meri- torious production, is true to nature, and will enhance the local reputation Mr. Beesley has already acquired as a landscape painter. A DESERTER AT RUNCORN —On Monday, James An- thony Crighton went to the Police Station and gave himself into the custody of Inspector Hollineworth as a deserter from the South Wales Borderers. He had, he stated, de- camped from the regiment's hospital with a suit of clothes. On Tuesday he was brought before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. W. Bankes, and committed to Knutsford Gaol to await an escort.

RUNCORN WANDERERS' BICYCLE CLUB —ln connection with this club a handicap race was run on the Aston Course, 41,- miles long, on Tuesday night, the starters being A. Stanway, scratch ; J. Bancroft and W. Woodward. 20 secs., J. Bate, 1 mm.; J. Green. 1 min 30 secs.; W. E. Fd,n, 1 mine. 45 secs.; and Thos. Fox. 2 mins. The race concluded as follows :—Green, 19 mine. 50 sees.; Eden, 19 mins. 55 sees; Bate. 20 mins 20 secs.; Fox. 20 mine. 20 sees: Wood- ward, 20 mine. 25 SPC9.; Bancroft, 0 mine. 30 secs. The first prize was an electro-plated teapot, valued at 40s. : 2nd, electro-plated breakfast cruet, valued at 225. 6d.; 3rd, a copper kettle. Mr. S. Sherlock acted as judge, and Mr. J. A.Rushton as starter and timekeeper. YOUTHFUL HOUSEBREAKERS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Thomas Feeley and James I Bowes,-boys under 12. were brought up on remand charged with breaking and entering the shop of Edward Johnson, provision dealer, Ann-street West, with intent to commit a felony.—Thomas Bums, manager to Mr. Johnson, said he secured the shop on Saturday rugnr auont a quartet eleven o'clock. Next morning at seven o'clock he azain visited the shop, and found the prisoners in the kitchen. He captured Feeley, but Bowes escaped. A quantity of goods had been moved, but he was unable to say that any had been stolen.—P.C. Snowden said. Bowes surrendered himself that morning.—The prisoners were remanded for a week.

HEARTLESS WIFE DESERTION AT WlDNES.—Yesterdav, at Widnes Police Court, Michael Melia, a labourer, w:ts charged, on remand, with deserting his wife.—From the evidence Of Mr. Scannell, it seemed that about July last the prisoner lived with his wife, who is 60 years of age. in a lodging-house in Widnes. He suddenly disappeared from the town, and as his poor wife had no money she was turned into the street. She was subsequently found by Mr. Scannell in a most pitiable condition, having scarcely suffi- cient clothing to cover her body. She was relieved by the Prescot Union at a cost of £2 is. 6, which was owing. The prisoner, although he had been in employment, had not for- warded a single penny for his wife's sustenance.—The Bench committed the prisoner to gaol for a month.

PERFORMANCE OF THE "PLOWER QUEEN" AT RUN- comc—The, beautiful descriptive cantata, " The Flower Queen," will be performed in Runcorn Public Hall, on Wednesday and Thursiay, the 14th and 15th instant, under the auspices of the Bethesda Congregational Chapel. A company of local female vocalists is busily engaged re- hearsing for the performance, under the conductorship of Mr. W. Handley, who is well qualified for such a task, and the bright music will receive an effective and attractive inter- pretation. The Queen elect will be Miss E. Eborall, a Liverpool soprano of considerable reputation, and the Recluse, Mr. Bantock Pierpoint, with whose excellencies the Runcorn public are well acquainted. The dresses and scenery will be on an extensive scale, and form a special feature in the representation of the " Coronation of the Rose."

SAVAGE ASSAULT ON A WOMAN AT WIDNES.—On Wed- nesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Julia Quinn and Patrick Quinn, mother and son, were charged with assaulting Rose A. Appleton, a widow, whom the superintendent of police described as a hard-working woman who maintained three chiliren by her own industry.—lt was alleged that when Mrs. Appleton was walking along Victoria-road, on the 20th August, Mrs. Quinn went up to her and without any provo- cation struck her on the forehead with a man's shoe. Com- plainant asked her motive for such conduct, when she knocked her down three times. Subsequently Patrick struck her on the head with a stone, inflicting a wound from which blood flowed freely.—Evidence bearing out this state- ment having been given, Supt. Barker said Mrs Quinn was a disorderly, violent woman—She was fined 20s. and costs, or a month's imprisonment, and her son was mulcted in the sum of 108. and costs, or, in default, 14 days. A VIOLENT WIDNES WOMAN.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Mary Fitz Patrick was summoned to answer a charge of committing a breach of the peace.—P.S. McGregor said on Thursday he and five other constables were maintainiug order in Legh-at. cut whiiet the WI" oje,-4,1 the defendant from a house for being in illegal possession of property. The defendant seized a bar of iron with which she attempted to strike the agent of the property, but she was placed outside, when she seized a mustard canister with the intention of striking witness. The witness, however, took it from her, and she endeavoured to create a riot amongst the large and "dangerous" crowd which had col- lected in the neighbourhood. He requested her to go away, but she became more violent, using very foul language, and several constables found it a difficult task to convey her to the police station.—The Bench ordered the woman to be bound over to keep the peace three months, herself in £lO and two sureties of £5 each, or go to gaol for a month. RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.—Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes judge, held a sitting at this court on Tuesday. The cause list included 47 original plaints. one adjourned plaint, and two judgment summonses. The only case of interest was one in which Mr. Burton, on behalf of Messrs. Simpson, Pavie-, and Co., sued William Bentham, a boatman for the sum of £9 17s id. Mr. 0. Leak defended. Defendant was the captain of a pair of the plaintiff's boats, and through his wife, to whom he entrusted all his business affairs, he had occasionally received loans from them. They were to be repaid from his wages. The present claim was made up of £4 7s ld overdrawn and £5 lOs for loans.—Defendant, while admitting that his wife managed his finances, stated that he was not aware of the debt until Wednesday, when his wife showed him the book (produced), from which it appeared that £2 12 was owing.—His Honour said the debt was clearly the defendant's, and he gave judgment for the plaintiffs.

RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.—The public of Runcorn who feel an interest in this most useful institution, will hear with regret that Mr. Charles Nickson has resigned the post of secretary, the duties of which office he has fulfilled with so much credit to himself and advan- tage to the association for the .past 18 months. At the con- clusion of the year-1881 the association, we may with truth state, was in a moribund condition. It was saddled with a debt of £5O. which there appeared no present hope of liqui- dating, the interest in its existence and labour was very slight, anerthe work done in its behalf was performed to a great extent in a perfunctory manner. The committee, however, determined to make one last effort, and Mr. Nick- son was appointed secretary, with anticipations that his energy and acquaintance with the town would stand the association in good stead. They we not disappointed. In less than 12 months, mainly through his energetic and per- sistent labours, the debt was cleared off, the association re- joiced in a surplus, and risen from the sleugh of despond into which it had fallen, fulfilled to a greater extent than formerly the object of its existence—" The improvement of the spiritual, mental, and social condition of young men." Mr. Nicksou has, however, through increasing business en- gagements, been compelled to resign his post, and he will lee succeeded by Mr. Kirkham Evans the assistant secretary, whom we trust may be as successful in his labours as his predecessor. Mr. C. Pownall is the assistant secretary. % RUNCORN STARR-BOWITETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—The second annual meeting of the Runcorn Starr-Bowkett Building Society was held last (Friday) night, when the fol- lowing report of t he directors was submitted and adopted:— The directors in their second annual report stated that during the past year the society had made considerable pro. gress in obtaining new members, and had attained a sound financial condition. As anticipated in the last report, the amount received in subscriptions showed a large increase. The directors urged upon the members that the success of the past year should be an incentive to the ape,. dy filling of the society, and that by the date of the annual meeting a vigorous effort should be made by each member to obtain as many new members as possible. Owing to removal from Runcorn, Mr. A. Campbell resigned his position as trustee. The directors requested Mr. J. R. Frith to undertake the duties pro tem., and they asked the members to appoint Mr. Frith in accordance with the provisions of Rule 9. During the year £730 had been advanced on property and secured by mortgage to the society, viz. :—Ooe leasehold dwelling- house, Westfield-road, Higher Runcorn, £300; Gne freehold house Bridgewater-street, Runcorn, £130; .three leasehold houses, Nelson-street, Widnes, £300; total, £730. Nine appropriations have already been made, four of ' which took place in the first year, four in the second year, and one during the present year, on which the society has just entered; those in the second year being as follows :—Fifch appropriation, amount £2OO, Mr. H. Randle; sixth appropriation, £lOO, Mr. W. Roach; seventh appropriation, £lOO, Miss A. M. Unswerth ; eighth appropriation, £lOO, Mr. T. T. Burrows. The fol- lowing directors haefulfilled their term of office, but were eligible for election :—Messrs. J. K. Digges T. Booth, J. D. Jones, and T. Riley. The balance sheet slowed that the • year was commenced with a balance in hand of £329 15s 101-d. The members' subscriptions amounted to £7BO Bs, the total receipts being £1,182 6s 2td. The expenditure, in- cluding a balance in the bank of £376 es, was the same amount. The liabilities were stated at £1,141 is. Messrs. Povak and W. Brookes certified the correctness of the - accounts.

LONDON IN AUTUMN—THE FLOWER BEDS IN THE PARKS—LONDON W AIFS—A GREAT DIS- COF pVERui%LOZ R _ _ET ILOvL‘ WITH H IP PEIITI."—TTHE R E FRENCH O AMBASSADOR HIS EXUta.,-unlTev THROWN OVER A WALL—EXPLANATIONS—ART OF THE COLONIES—THE HAUNTED HOUSE IN BERKELY- SQU ARE.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

Sir Charles Dilke says, and not only preaches the doctrine but practices it, that there is no place like London in Sep- tember. Of late years a knowledge of what the metropolis is like at that period of the year has been forced upon legislators. There were happy times, not further back than seven or eight years, when Parliament was invariably pro- rogued in or about the first week in August. To sit on the twelfth was to the great body of members a much more shocking thing even than sitting two hours into Sunday morning was to the pure mind and strict views of Mr. Callan. Now, it is something to be thankful for if work is done before the end of August, and a shadow is removed from life when it is fully ascertained that there is to be no autumn session. There is hanging about London just now a strangeness of aspect which supplies the quality of variety sought for by wearied workers. A man accustomed to London in the season would find as many new things now as he might hope to discover in a lengthy term of travel. There is about the streets a curious sense of quiet- nesi which is drowsily soothing. Taking •a walk down Piccadilly or up Bond-street we seem to have come into a land where it is always Sunday afternoon. The shops are open it is true. But where are the well-dressed throng, the long lines of carriages and the beatific views of powdered heads and flesh-coloured calfs ? Jeames has gone with his master and mistress, and is recruiting his wearied energies amid country air, and with the advantage of earlier hours. One thing missed by the people who have hastened away from London because the season and the session are over, are the flower beds in the parks and public, gardens. These are jest now at their best, glorying in the sunshine which haa halrPti fnr nncitiVeiV three weeks. A. "•".- bountifully and regularly watered, they are making the best of both condition, having sun by day and a substitute for rain at night. TLe flower beds lie in great masses of colour in the parks, and if society has gone out of town regardless of these delights, it is well to know that a class of people who more greatly need them are revelling in them. Perhaps in the season we cannot see the working classes because of the finer feathers of richer folk. Perhaps they do not come then, shrinking from the contrast and the companionship. Just now they turn out in large numbers, and all the parks East and West, more especially-on a Sunday, have crowds of enthusiastic admirers of their beauty.

There is a little bit of garden ground, perhaps the most obscure in London. since it leads to nowhere but Vauxhall Bridge. It lies on the embankment by the Victoria Tower of the Houses of Parliament—a mere strip of garden land, but green with grass and gay with flowers. The other even- ing I was walking that way behind a group of five of about the dirtiest and most utterly neglected children London could produce. The oldest was about seven and the youngest three. He had, I fancy, been washed three times in his earthly career, and the anniversary was close at hand. Presently they came to the bit of garden, and the older boy, running forward and scrambling up by the rail- ings, cried out, "I say ! Here's the country !" The excite- ment was intense. The group dashed forward. Young Three-year-old was lifted up en to the stone boundary to share the bliss, and they stood there gazing upon this un- known land which they had sometimes heard vaguely alluded to as "the country," and which apparently they now beheld for the first time. Stout Cortez, when with eagle eyes
He stared at the Pacific, and all his men look'd at each other with a wild surmise—

Silent, upon a peak, in Darien, was not in a condition of sublimer surprise or more ecstatic delight than these five mangey crows of London child life. The succession of the Comte de Paris to the heritage of the Comte de Chambord is a very serious thing for the claims of Prince Vietor Napoleen to the throne of France. That sooner or later, and sooner rather than later, the Republic will be displaced is a fact that must be admitted even by those who politically regret it most. There have been many Republics in France since 1789, and they have all gone the one way. The present one, founded upon the ruins of the third Empire, has existed so long only by acci- dent. There have been more than one distinctly recognised epoch when accident has prevented the inevitable catas- trophe. The death of Gambetta" was the cutting away of the last hope of a prolongation of the Republic. Knowing Gambetta personally, and being intimately acquainted with his home policy, I have not the slightest doubt that with him the Republic would have been maintained only just so long as must have intervened before he was ready to play the part of the First Consul. Since his death a succession of incompetent Ministers have brought the Republic into deeper discredit. There is growing up in France a feeling that for its own safety's sake the sooner it is done with the congeries of conflicting small personal interests and petty ambitions which pass under the name of a Ministry the better. Had the Prince Imperial been alive, especially if be had come back from South Africa with the military prestige his fearless character would .have earned for him, he would now have been seated on the throne of his father. As it is the conflict lies between the scion of an unpopular branch of the Bonaparte family and the descendant of Louis Pbillippe, who now unites in himself the heritage both of the elder and younger branch of the Bourbons. The odds are at present in favour of the Comte de Paris, one of the most ! unfortunate things in connection with him being his Christian names. One Louis Phillippe has been enough for France.

There is a story current about the Prince of Wales which is so unlike his habitual tact and good sense- that though it has been whispered about for some time it has not seemed worthy ef credence. The other night I met one of the parties in the not very clever farce and gathered that the story cannot be denied. The affair happened just before the Prince left for the continent, and whilst he was visiting the Isle of Wight, I A lady well-known in London society has a house down there, and it was the height of her ambition to entertain the Prince of Wales. Her importunity prevailed, and the Prince not only accepted the invitation, but sent a polite note to enquire whether he might bring with him the French Ambassador? This doubled the delight of the worthy hostess, and an effusive assent was returned. In due time the Prince of Wales appeared with a small personal entocrage, including Lord Charles Beresford and the French Ambassador. There was a distingnished company present to meet the Prince, amongst them a gallant English admiral, small in stature, but heroic in soul. In the cflurse of the conversation the French Ambassador, with astonishing variation from diplomatic courtesy, began to speak dis- respectful of the English navy. He declared that ene French ironclad would clear the Channel of three English, and that man for man the French sailor would make mince- meat of the British. The gallant admiral ligened to this conversation with growing restlessness. Ile did not like to argue with the representative of a foreign Power in the presence of the Prince of Wales. But the Frenchman con- tinuing with increased offensiveness the Admiral struck in.

The altercation grew in height and anger. The group surrounding the controversialists moved towards the garden and presently there reached the hostess a re ort that the admir..l and the French Ambassador were fighting. This was quickly followed by a still more alarming report that the French Ambassador had been thrown over the wall, and that his leg was broken. Such a contretemps happening in her house on an oceasion when the Prince of Wales was present added to her distra otion which was only varied when the Prince of Wales suggested that the French Ambassador always drank Absinthe, and that some might now do him good. There was none in the House, and messengers were sent all over Hyde in search of the curative compound. Meanwhile the French Ambassador was milled off, the , breathless and secretly frightened British Admiral also retired, and the party broke up. Whether the lady was consoled when a day or two later she learned that the whole thing was a joke, that the French Ambassador was none other than a well-known Special Correspondent, who has more than once been the companion of the Prince of Wales in foreign towns, is a matter of doubt, What the Admiral thought of the matter, .what will be the view of M. Wad- dington and the French people when the story reaches their ears, and whether, on the whole, the recreations of Prince Hal with Falstaff and his other boon companions were better or worse than this, are all interesting questions.
It is pleasant to see that our Colonists are cultivating a taste for the fine arts. Commissions have been frequently hgiven of late to sculptors and painters in this country for

statues and pictures for the decoration of public buildings in one or other ef our distant colonies. The meat recent is that entrusted to Signor Fontana, for three full-sized figures in Carrara marble, to be placod in the halls of the Govern- ment Offices in Sydney. The statues, which are now com- pleted and on view at the sculptor's studio in Chelsea, are those of the Queen and the Prince of Wales; and an alle- gorical reprogentcition of New South Wales. They are re- markably fine works of art. The Queen wears the crown and. robes of State, the Riban.d of the Garter, and the Star of India. The likeness is considered an excellent one, and an air of majesty and repose surrounds it. The Prince, of Wales is in the uniform of a Field Marshal, and the details have all been minutely observed. This part is also said to be very good. The figure representing New South Wales is a masterpiece of art. It is that of a youthful female classically draped and crowned with a garland of Australian Flora, surmounted with the rays of the rising sun. Orte of the arms encircles a trophy of canals and fruits, the hand of the other holds a wreath, while at her feet lies a ram in all the glory of his wool—the mineral wealth of the colony being typified by a nugget of gold. These works are alike a credit to the sculptor and to the colony to which they are destined.

There has been a rumour lately that the Haunted House in Berkeley Square is to let, and the result has been a con- stant stream of enquirers at the grim-looking corner house, next door to Lord Strathnairn's. It seems simultaneously to have occurred to a good many shrewd people that a bar- gain was to be had. There are 'many who would not care to live in a haunted house, and with the circle of possible tenants thus restricted the rent would be exceptionally low. But all these hopes have been doomed to disappointment. The door is opened by a slatternly-looking woman who, in reply to the enquiry "Is this house to let?" sharply answers "No, it ain't," and forthwith slams the daor in the face of the bona—fide traveller to Berkeley Square in search of a residence. It is curious to come upon this house in a fashionable square, with all the fronts of its neighbours clean and bright with curtains and window gardening, and cif night lit up and full of life, whilst the corner house, day and night, reivntuu „ vet penetrated the mystery. All that is known is that about nine years ago the house was taken from Lord Fitzharding on a long lease; furniture was brought in, there were ser- vants about and one middle—aged lady, who seemed the proprietor. Then suddenly the blinds were drawn, dirt and silence reigned, and no one has ever been seen to enter or leave the house.

div.p: RUNCORN RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIA-
TION.

A special meeting of the members of this association was held in Bethesda School-room on Tuesday evening last—Mr. U. Coleburn in the chair—when there was a goodly number present, the object of the meeting being to consider what action should be taken in view of the forthcoming election of Commissioners. The Beasley case formed the piincipal topic of discussion, and a variety of opinions was expressed on the subject, but all agreed in the main that the Com- missioners were very much to blame in their management of the case. The attempt which has been made to saddle upon one or two of the Commissioners the whole of the blame did not meet with much favour, as their action was endorsed and sanctioned in the regular way by the Board ; but as to whether the procedure the Commissioners took was based upon the advice of their law clerk was a point upon which the meeting could not decide for want of further in- formation. It was explained on behalf of the committee that a deputation had been appointed, and had waited upon Mr. Linaker in order to inspect the bill of costs, but without the authority of the chairman of the Board Mr. Linaker did not feel himself at liberty to show the bill to the deputation. The action of some of the Commissioners in turning tale upon the general body and offering to give evidence on behalf of Mr. Beasley was strongly condemned. Ultimately it was decided that the association should not support the return of any of the retiring Commissioners, who are all more or less res- ponsible for the result of the Beasley case. It was there- fore agreed that the association should bring forward two new candidates and ask the ratepayers to support them as a protest against the blundering of the Commissioners in the case alluded to, at the same time leaving the ratepayers free to select any three of the retiring members whom they may prefer to return on the Board.—Messrs. F. Fairhurst and IL White were the gentlemen selected, both of whom have consented to stand. Communicated.

TRH CHARGB Ow TNESPASS AGAINST AN ASTON FAR- IOM'S ON.—Joseph Wilkinson, a young man, again appeared at the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on :londay, to answer a charge of trespassing in search of game on land at Aston Grange, in the occupation ot Colonel Talbot, on the 22nd June.—Mr. Hitchen appeared to prosecute, and Mr. W. H. Litigter defended. A somewhat heated legal argu- ment took place between these gentlemen, awl ultimately Mr. Linaker called for the production of the cotnplainant's deed of title': Mr. Hitchen said he might ask for it but he would not get it.—The Bench said the complainant nit having produced his title the case was dismissed. Mr. Linaker applied for costs, which were refused.

div.head: RUNCORN RECHA.BITES' DEMO.NSTRATION.
div.p: RUNCORN RECHA.BITES' DEMO.NSTRA- TION.

The members of the 1--.l;c:n- Tent No. 215 (adults) and gxcelsior Tent (juveniles) of the lniependent Order of Rechabites held their annual deinonetration on Mon.lay last. The weather was beautifully fine, and the members net at Bethesda School-room in coneilerable numbers to take part in the procession through the town. The adult tent was represented by 50 members, and the jiivenile tent by 60 members They started from the echoel at half-pist two, headed ky the Star of Widnes Temperance Brass Band, and a handsome two-poled banner. 1'4)110e:rm.; were Bras. Wilson, DI) R.' I'. F. Lea, P.C.R., J. Dimond, P.H.C.R. (of Southport), H. Hinds, D.T., Jec., all wearing the badge of the Order. The juveniles carried bannerettes of various rie,igns. Brother S. Lamh, P.D C R., of Widnes, marshalled the adult section, and Brother R. Evans and James Lea (superintendents) the juvenile section. The procession wended its way direct to Halton, where they were joined by 20 members of the Halton tent, led by Brother W. H. Brad- bury, the secretary, and after parading the village a field provided by the Halton brethren was occupied, and sports engaged in. Halton was left behind at four o'clock, and the procession, by way of Bridge, Church, and King-streets,' visited Dr. Robinson's residence, where the band played a selection of music. Then along Lord-street, Ashridge-street, Waterloo Bridge, and Lowlands-road, until the Cocoa Rooms were reached, when another stop- page was made. Brook-street, Egerton-street, Devon- shire-square, and High-street were paraded, a stoppage being made at Dr. MacDougall's residence and the Temperance Hotel. Arriving at the Bethesda school, tea, to which about 250 persons sat down, was partaken of, and subsequently a public meeting was held, presided over by Mr. W. Parish, J.P., of Chester. He was supported on the platform by Bros. Dimond, Dutton, Hinds, Lamb, Wil- eon, Caleb Hart, Ric'eard Evans, and J. E. Warburton (secretary). The room was crowded to excess. The Chairman having delivered a sbott address, Mr. J. E War- burton gave a report. He stated the tent was opened on the 23rd October, 1873, with 23 members, and although it encountered many vicissitudes it had slowly advanced in strength and usefulness. In 1881 the membership was 63, which had increased in 1882 to 84, while at the present time it stood at 98. At the close of 1881 the money value of the tent was £202 is 214. ; 1882, £232 10s. 51-1.; increase £3O 9s 3d. This min was simply used to meet all claims for sickness, and to pay the management expenses, all pay- ments for deaths being made by the district tent, to which the subordinate tents made an anaual contribution. The average worth per member was at the close of 1882, £2 15s. 41d., white at the ee-- r--2 .• " . . 0. 0,1 r momb‘r, a maca Limner average than usual. Toe average of a non-temperance society in the locality was 12a. id, so that the Rechabites occupied a very favourable position. (Applause.) For the seven years ending 1882, the Runcorn Rechabites' tent paid for sickness an average of ss. 3d. per member, while the average paid during the same period by the other society he had men- tioned was no less than us. 7d. per member, or more than double the Rechabites. (Applause.) The average number of days sickness in the whole of the Rechabite Order was a little under six, and of the other order he had named the average was ten days. The Rechabites, therefore, had cause for gratification. Mr. Warburton then gave a detailed statement of the contributions and benefits of the Rechabite Order, and the advantages of membership was very apparent. —Mr. R. EVANS, superintendent of the juvenile tent, said the tent over which he presided was in ,a dying state in March 1881, only having three members, but by dint of hard work and plodding perseverance, the number had increased to 58 in the present month, and twelve had been added that day, making the total number of members 70. He urged the parents present to enrol their children, thus training them in temperance principle., and obtaining for them the benefits of a valuable institution. By the payment of 7d. per month they were entitled to 3s. per week for 16 weeks, when the amount would be reduced to Is. 6d. for a further 16 weeks, and if the illness still continue to Is. per week so long as the member remained in that condition. In case of deaths the member's representative was entitled to £3. Members as soon as initiated were entitled to medical aid free of charge. At the age of 16 the members were transferred to the adult tent.—Bro. Dimond, Bro. Dutton, and Bro. Hinde gave addresses appropriate to the occasion, showing the ad- vantages offered by the society with which they were con- nected, and advocating strongly total abstinence from in- tdxicating liquors.—During the evening the band played selections of music. Bro. Mathias Stephens gave a recita- tion, and Bros. John Leach and Wesby Haddock gave a re- citation, entitled "Rechabite facts." Bro. Fred Leach and Miss Maria Parr each sang a song. The members of the juvenile tent, assisted by the members of St. John's Band of Hope, sang "Who is that brave man, who ? " Bro. Caleb gave a recitation in the Lancashire dialect in an ex- cellent manner, and he was encored. He kindly responded by a second recitation.—The meeting concluded by Bro. Dutton pronouncing the Benediction.

' The Rev. W. Vause, who succeeds the Rev. J. Billington in the pastorate of the Runcorn circuit of the United Methodist Free Church. commenced his labours on Sunday last. In the morning he preached to a good congregation at the Zion Church, Widnes, and in the evening he occupied the pulpit at Ellestnere-street Church, Runcorn. On Mon- day evening a successful tea party was held in the school belonging to the Runcorn church, the ladies presiding at the tablis being Mesdames White, 'retnperley, E. Jones, Clarke, J. ALLEGED BURGLARY AT WIDNES.

SHARP CAPTURE. Before Mr. F. H. Gossage, at Widoes Police Court, on Tueiday, William Furber, a young man about 18 years of was brought up on remand charged with burglariously entering the Angel Hotel, Mersey-read, Widnes, and steal- ing therefrom £47 16s 3d ; jewellery, consisting of one gold guard, two silver guards, one diamond ring, one silver rine., one keeper ring, one silver brooch, one pair of eye &sae's, worth about £l3; and nine purses, and a few other odd artic:es. The facts of the case, as contained in the evidence of P.C.'s Laing and Thompson, and Mrs. Mary Sutton, widow, the landlady of the house, seem to be these: About half- past two o'clock on Monday morning, P.C. Laing was pass- ing the Angel Hotel, when he heard a low whistle, and a voice say "Tom." He looked round to discover whence the noice proceeded, and perceived that the. cellar grid did not occupy its usual place. To the better aid in his investi- gations be struck a light, and whilst peering into the dim recesses he heard footsteps across the cellar floor. He whistled for assistance, and P.C. Thompson was quickly on the spot. While Thomp3on guarded the outlet, Laing descended the cellar, and found the prisoner concealed on the top of the stairs leading into the kitchen. He asked " What are you doing here? " and the prisoner replied "I only wanted a drink of beer." Thompson, however, took charge of the prisoner, and Laing having awakened Mrs. Sutton, exaipined with her the cellar. On a beer barrel he found a- handkerchief containing £36 16s 3d in money—which included two LW Bank of England notes, ten XI packages of gold and silver, the remainder being in various purses and loose, and the jewellery men- tioned in the charge. After Mrs. Sutton had identified the Property the prisoner was taken to the police station, where £4 in gold rolled up in a piece of cloth was found in his left boot, and £7 concealed between the linings of his coat. He made no answer to the charge, but when being taken to the cells he said "That handkerchief belongs to me ; it is my property; give it to me." Laing and Thompson then made a re-examination of the hotel premises. It appears that "more out of charity than anything else "Mrs. Sutton had occasionally employed the prisoner, who was therefore well acquainted with the entire house, and Mrs. Sutton's habit. He effected an entrance by removing the cells- grid, and by means of a joiner's paring chisel and a "coal chisel," he smashed open the trap-door leading into the cellar. Wood had also been cut away from the lock of the door leading from the beer cellar to the wine cellar. He then discovered the writing desk containing the money and valuables, and having tied them up in the handkerchief, was apparently about to make his exit when the constable VirliarcUirge),lnlllllrNTaraniiiiitrea'. thaPaTilluitk next Liverpool Assizes.

div.head: RUNCORN, WESToN, AND HALTON WATERWORKS CoMP.kNY,
div.p: RUNCORN, WESToN, AND HALTON WATERWORKS CoMP.kNY,

The half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of this com- pany was held at the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Monday afternoon. Mr. John Brundrit, the chairman of directors, presided. There were present Messrs. W. Hayes, T.Bankes, ' W. Whittaker, James Collier, P. Smith, E. Timmins, James Shaw, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary).—The directors' report, which was published in The Examiner last Saturday, was t iken as read.—The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report and the payment of a dividend of 4 per cent. per annum, remarked that through illness he was unfortu- nately unable to be present at the last half-yearly meeting, but he was well represented by one of his brother directors. At that meeting they were only able to declare a dividend of 3!i per cent. That aiose from the fact that during the last three months of 1882 the season was very wet, which caused the large consumers to take less quantities of water than usual. To some extent a similar state of things existed in the first three months of this year, and militated against the success of the company. The last three months, when they had had seasonable summer weather, had placed the company in a flourishing condition, and the inereased income made up what in the first three months seemed a deficiency. During the quarter ending March 31st the amount received for water rents was £756 2s 10d, which" in the ensuing quarter had increased to £1,055 14s id, or nearly 50 per cent. This showed the difference a wet or a dry season made to the company. From the report of the secretary there was every prospect that the forthcoming half year would be a successful one, the dry weather having favoured them. Referring to the leakage in the reservoir, the Chairman said after consulta- tion with Mr. Timmins, who was a practical man, a scheme had been adopted which while it would not interrupt the supply of water to the town would cost very little. The ' machinery and plant of the company were in good order, the water continued abundant in the well, and that it was , of excellent quality was attested by the several sanitary I authorities with whom they were brought in contact.—Mr. BASHES seconded the motion, which was carried.—On the motion of Mr. HaYEs, seconded by Mr. Wurrraxun, the retir- ing dirt-ctors,Mr. Rinkes and Mr. Tinunins,were re-appointed. The CHAIRMAN said it would be necessary to appoint an auditor in place of Mr. R. Forrester, who, having withdrawn his interest from the company, was no longer qualified to act.—Mr. HayEs proposed, and Mr. Sitaw seconded, the appointment of Mr. Robert Foulkes.—The motion was unanimously carried.—Mr. SHAW moved, and Mr. COLLIER seconded, a vote of thanka to the chairman, which was car- ried.—lp reply, the CHAIRMAN expressed his obligations for the honour they had done him, and assured the meeting that the directors would always do the best they could for the interest of the shareholders. He trusted that the altera- tions in the management and other improvements would, while causing a perceptible increase in the ince me, uete ease - from the report that there had been a diminution in the exp,nditure. While in the half-year ending June 30th, 1882, the expenses were £BO2 is 6d, in the last half-year they had been reduced to .E 773 Os 6d. The interest paid in the first-named half-year was £592 Gs 2d, now reduced to £575 2s 2.1. This showed a satisfactory state of affiirs, and the directors looked hopefully to the future.—Mr. COLLIER moved, Mr. SHAW seconded, and the CHAIRMAN in eulogistic terms supported, evote of thanks to the secretary. No body of directors, it was observed, could have a more willing and obliging s,!.cretary, or one who had more at heart the interests of the company.—The motion was carried, and Mr. Salkeld having replied, the meeting terminated.

div.head: FRUIT BANUU.E,T AT RUNCORN.
div.p: FRUIT BANUU.E,T AT RUNCORN.

The annual fruit banquet and entertainment in connec- tion with the Runcorn Young Men's Christian Associa- tion was held in Bethesda schoolroom on Thursday evening. Dr. Steele, the president of the association, occupied the chair. The arrangements were similar to those of former years, but, unfortunately, the company which assembled did not number more than a hundred persons, and iinanci- ally the affair was not a success. Placed along the centre if the room was a long table, decorated with handsome ferns, and beautiful flowers, which had been kindly lent or given by Mrs. C. Hazlebnrst, Mrs. Wigg, Mr. P. Speakman, Mr. J. 0. Jackson, and Mr. Yapp, of H.dton. It was well laden with fruit of all descriptions, from the luscious grape to the green apple. A cross table near the platform was laid out in a similar mariner. To add to the evening's enj7mtnt, an excellent musical programme had been pro- vided. It opened with a part song, "Relieve me of all those endearing young charms." which was tunefully sung by Mr. C. Pownall, Miss Wright, and others. Mr. C. Pewnall sung with taste and good expression the song "Good company; " and Miss Wright succeeded in obtain- ing an encore for her capital rendering of " Ehren on the Rhine." Later in the evening Miss Wright was again en- cored for her interpretation of " The two little .spoons," and to the delight of the audience she repeated the two last verses. The duet " When the wind bloweth in from the fi:a," was givm in good style by Miss Horton and Mr. R. Morris. Miss Jukes, who performed the duties of accom- panist, gave in her usual skilful manner a piano- forte soy. ; and Miss Horton, who possesses a clear, expressive voice sang " As I'd nothing else to do," for which she was loudly applauded. "The bellringer "by Mr. R. Mortis was much appreciated. The programme con- cluded with the part song "The sun smiles in beauty" by the glee party. During the evening Mr. T. W. Gladstone, organisin, agent of the Young Men's Christian Association for the midland district, gave an address, in which he dealt with the aim and work of Young Men's Christian Associa- tions in a manner which met with much acceptance.

of this Board was held at the The monthly meetin• . offices, Victoria-road, ont'Thu:rsday, Mr. Bradshaw presiding. LT. T Rev. Father Clarke, Dr. There were also present the O'Keeffe, Messrs. H. W. Deacon Brunner, W. Shaw,,. Davies, and Danby (clerk). tcs. IMPORTANT EDUCATIONAL SrATIO:.

The District Education Committee repqnod hat during the month of July (three weeks) 203 persotsr appez,.-ed be- fore them for contravention of the Eduction Act, ern: 98 applied for fees. Fees were recommended to be paid in 65 cases, and 31 persons were prosecuted before the magistrale,4; Convictions were obtained in 30 cases.—Mr. H. W. I.)Naoox, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said that during the holidays the attendance officers of the Board had been employed in taking a census of the children of the district. The number of houses in the district was 5,088, against 5,091 last year; but Um number of inhabited houses, however, had increased from 4,262 last year to 4,308 this year. This was a rather striking fact, especially when they considered the number of children between the ages of three and thirteen, which was 6,250 against 6,236 last year. This was a very small increase in the number of children, but there had been a consiaerable increase in the number of inhabited houses. He drew the attention of the officers to this point, and they said they had noticed in taking the census that there were fewer families living together in one house this year than last. The number of children between the ages of three and 13 not attending school was 1,155 against 1,277 last year, so that there was a considerable decrease in the number of children who were not attending school, which was a very satisfactory fact. The number of children b3tween the ages of three and five was 1,327; last year 1,415. There were fewer children not on the rolls who ought to be than last year, the numbers being 185 at the present time and 194 last year. This was larger than the committee ex- /anted. He went through the books, and found that a largo proportion of these children had just turned five—that in fact nine out of ten, or he might go further and say nineteen out of twenty were between the ages of five and six. The number of children attending school, but not living in the Own, was 102, as compared with 85 last year; whilst the number of children on the rolls of the public elementary schools on June 30th was 5,244, being almost identical with last year, which was 5,247. Reckoning the population of Widnes as 26,000, the proportion of school-goins children was 1 to s.7o.—The report was adopted.

THE BOARD AND StADAY CLOSING. A letter was read from the committee of the E:ete of In. toxicatin, Liquors on Sunday Bill, enclosing a ntmorial Board's the ard's adoption in favour of that measure.— Mr. DEACON Said the Board had no power to deal with such a matter.—Mr. &taw said the question was a simple one. It was, did they, as members of that Board, coesider that the sale of intoxicating liquors on the Sibbath had any injuri- ous effect either upon the work of the Board or upon4ho population? They must, he thought, oetne to the conelu- sion that there was something injurioue in that sale, and a. preventitive measure would be a benefit to all parties con- cerned—not only to the children, but te their parents, and he believed that the liquor trade would also receive a benefit- by a cessation of labour. Under these circumstances he did not see that the Board was departing from its duty by signing the petitim, which he moved should be done.—Mr. BuuNNER-seconded.—Mr. DEACON moved an amendment that the petition lie upon the table. The Board was there to manage the ratepayers schools; the members were elected to carry en the educa- tion of the children in the district on certain Rfinite lines, and it did not come within their scope to giva an opinion upon the subject of the sale of intoxicating liqcors on Sun- day.—Dr. O'KEEFE seconded the amendment, not because he did not consider what Mr. Shaw had said was laudable, but because he agreed with Mr. Deacon that the Board ought , not to interfere in any matters which did not concern the education of the children entrusted to their care.—Mr. DAVIES remarked that the Sunday traffic in intoxicating liquor, especially in a place like -Widnes, had a demoralis- inte effect, and he strongly advocated the signing of the petition.—Mr. SHAW said he had no doubt that the fees the Board had to pay in 98 cases last montll,was mainly owing to the drink traffic. He was satisfied that the amount of wages workmen received was ample to keep the population well clothed and well fed, and Pay the sdhool fees for their children if it were not for the temptations placed in their way by the public-houses on Sundays.—Father CLARKE denied that in toto that the workingmen in Widnes had sufficient wages to pay school fees and keep themselves and families well clothed and well fed.—The amendment was defeated by four votes to three, and the original resolution being put as a substan- tive motion, was carried by four votes to two, Father Clarke ahstainin,, frOMIVOULIZ TI E PROl'LMEllretLzc UIIIOES.

Allen, clerk to the Widnes Local Board, with reference to providing public offices, which subject was under the consideration of the Local Board, asking if he would let him know what accommodation the School Board would require.— Mr. SHAW said the Finance Committee had replied, and he spoke of the ad. - vantages which would accrue from a concentration of the public offices in one building.—Dr. O'KEEFE spoke in the same strain.—Mr. DEACON said he did not think the School Board would be justified in removing, unless the Local Board would accommodate them as cheaply as they were at nresent.—The matter then ceased.

OUR NATIONAL CHURCH. Sir,—ln reading the letters that have appeared on this subject, I have noticed your corresnondent, " H. J. West- brook," has completely' ignored questions which have been asked respecting his reckless assertions, but it seems when a simple statement of fact is made he cannot accept it without the proofs he himself is unwilling to furnish. However, for the edification of your correspondent,l may state that I did go "right in" the church to a spot which commanded a full view of the edifice, that the curate's name was Jones, that the service was held about the beginning of this year, and that notwithstanding his enquiries the statement that only two persons were present is perfectly true. On care- fully reading the letter signed "H. J. Westbrook," I have become curious as to the authorship, and have wondered whether Mr. Westbrook's share is not confined to making a 4' fair copy "of, and signing his name to them, for some- how I get—to quote your correspondent's words—" con- firmed in my belief" that the hand is the hand of Esau, but the voice is Jacob's voice.—l am, sir, ke., Warrington, August 29, 1883. VISITOR.

Sir,—The several Letters which have appeared in The Examiner on this subject I have read with much interest, but they seem to me to represent a controversy between op- posed religions organisations than to go to the root of the (ipestion as to the necessity of a national church having any ittst claims to exist in these our times. Ido not now pro- fess to deal with that myself, and would ask permission to ; take notice only of the reference made by Mr. Westbrook to the attendance at village churches as an argument for the State Church. Now, as a matter of fact, is that attendance all spontaneous, or is it not largely the result of social and sacredatal in- fluence ? I know something of village life. and I proceed to relate this circumstance :—I was residing with my family in a village, where there was a email church and no other public place of worship. We all attended the services of the church, and we were on friendly terms with the clergymen, which were cemented by • my being able, in a bumble way, to advise his wife (who was the organist) on choir matters and organ music. About T fishl her Ins, gardener that a little building near was to be used, by some pious people from the neighbouring town, for evangelical services on Sunday evening during the summer months. I was at the opening with some of my family and two friends who were staying with us, and there were present about 15 or eo of miserable peasants such as I bad nexer seen in the church ;*they were, indeed, of the class who shrink, in their poverty, from mingling there with the better-ead miserable sinners. From that day I and iny wife experienced a re- markable change in the demeanour of the clergyman and his wife towards us—which I was perfectly indifferent about, but which I thought mean and sorrowful. Well, we made up a party among ourselves every Sunday evening to go to this little unpretentious building, and we felt happy in giving en- couragement to so commendable an effort for good—for it reached the desolate and miserable. We continued, of course, our attendance at the church at some of the ser- vices; but soon I was called away abroad on business for a few months, and heard nothing as to how affairs religious were faring in my little village. On my return I was told by my wife that our countenance of the little Bethel had given mortal offence to the two prominent individuals above named, arid that she had been passed by even on the road And elsewhere with contempt. Happily, she was of thst temperament not to care a fig about that treatment, but in my opinion unwisely continued her attendance with the family at the church. I severed it, however, with her con- currence, and wrote a courteous, but firm, letter to the jealous parson. giving him my reasons for so doing. I then made it my business to enquire generally at the cottages throughout the district as to the extent of their freedom in spiritual matters, when I discovered the disgraceful fact that it was comparatively nil. I have in other secluded districts made the same searching inquiries, and I have found the same repressive influences in active operation. As I had worshipped in the Church of England nearly all my life, and given some special services (about which I speak with real modesty) to the churches wherever I have been located, I feel that I have some right to speak upon this question. • M. A VINDITI ATION. Sir,—With regard to the report of the case, Lee v. Mit- chell and Nephew, in your issue of the 25th inst., I ask you in the name of justice to insert the following facts. In the first place, we had no books whatever from the woman Lee. She was waited upon by our canvasser, who stated his busi- ness, at the same time giving her a circular in which our terms were clearly stated. She requested him to call that day week. The appointment was kept, when she placed a list of debts in his hand, asking at tlee same time if we pur- chased debts, to which he replied, "Our principal buys debts occasionally after they have been submitted to him ana met with his approval, but with that I have nothing to do; my business is to canvass for debts to be collected." Now, sir, we had been at work for several days sending out notices by post to the debtors, and one of our firm was engaged certifying to the debts. Some of the parties who. had received our notice went at once to the plaintiff Lee, gave her monsy on account, aud made terms for future payments. Her object thus accomplished, she wrote to us demanding the restoration of her debt list and of all moneys collected. There had been but one debt collected, which was offered her less our commission and fivepence on the notices. I can assure you that bad his Honour allowed the case to proceed, we were prepared to prove every word here stated, and refute the virulent statement made by plaintiff's solicitor.—We are, sir, yours, &c., MITCHELL & NEPHEW. 15, Upper Bank-street, Warrington, August 28th.

"A National Church is a national possession not lightly' to be parted with, for by centuries of gradual growth it has intertwined itself into the very heart of the nation." Sir,—Having divided my letter into two parts, it may not be out of place if I give some additional statistics regateling the Church of England, both as to how far it represents the nation, and to the progress it ha e made within the last few years. It has been gathered that out of every 100 of the population, school returns show 72 Church- men, marriage 75 ditto, navy 75 ditto, army 63 ditto, cemeteries (buried in) 70 ditto, and workhouses 79 ditto ; so that the result of a real religious census . would probably show three-fourths of the people to be Churchmen. Since the diocese of Manchester was founded in 1817, 200 new churches have been built. That is exclusive of the 38 old churches, which have been restored and enlarged. According to the report of the National Society it appears that the accommodation provided in the Church schools last year was, in round numbers, for 2,400 000 scholars, or nearly doable that provided by the School Board, and nearly a quarter of a million in excess of the " total " accommoda- tion of the Board schools, the British, Wesleyan, and Roman Catholic schools combined. Noble figures when it is remembered that all this education is provided by the "voluntary" contributions of Churchmen. Speaking of voluntary schools, the Times of June 13th says :—" It is not indeed wholly impossible that the rivalry of the two systems (School Boards and voluntary schools) may some day result in a reaction in favour of voluntary schools as against the increasing expenditure and growing ambition of Board schools." The increase of scholars in church schools last year was 48,000, as against i 19,000 n 1881. The Church of England spends nearly £600,000 annually in support of its voluntary schools. From an article on confirmation statistics in the Church Quarterly Review, the Rev. W. A. Whitworth draws the following conclusions : "That in 25 dioceses, while the total number of children annually arriving ..t confirmation ao,s is 394,000, there are 272,000 Church of England children of age to be confirmed, and 170,000 children annually receive confirmation; so that while the Church possesses 69 per cent, of the population, more than one-halt of the female population, and more than one-third of the male population are being confirmed." From correspor.idence on the Church in Wales. which has been going on in Church Bell, we gather, says the "National Church" of July last, that the rising generation is returning in large numbe,re to the church of their fathers, which the increase in confirma- tion candidates kfrom 4,000 Po 7,000 in three years in the Diocese of St. David's) strikingly illustrates. Interpenetrating this mirth, comes occasionally and briefly the deeper ha! ha! of a male voice harmoniously mingling: the first belongs to Miss Frances Vandeleur ; the last to Stephen. As we look in upon them, a pretty scene meets the eye. , The walls, windows, cornice, and chandelier of the billiard room are wreathed and garlanded with green and variegated ivies; while the wall at the farther end is pierced by three graceful arches, a tall centre one, and a smaller one at each side. Through these (the doors having been removed for the occasion) the eve ranges in delight along the vista of ch. ......rvatory, which appears here in its extreme length, full of the cuoi,...t ~rsa flowora Is.orru tv horticultural world. Baskets, pendant from the roof, and so profuse in their floral wealth that their luxuriance threatens inconvenience to tall passers-by, alternate with transparent, fairy-like globes; that were to-night• to have shed their soft splendour on the captivating scene, but which will then share the darkness of all around them.

Turning to the wall behind us, we are for a moment sub- jected to a charming illusion—the extension of the cinser- vatory through a similar series of arches, and a far-reach- ing vista corresponding with the opposite end of the room, but which is only the reflection of the latter from a large mirror. _ _ _

Miss Vandeleur, a figure of medium height, and ex- quisitely-rounded form, as the plain, close-fitting, light blue dress makes apparent, is passing to and from the conserva- tory with a small basket on her arm ; fetching flowers to 'light up,' as she says, the wilderness of foliage,' left by the servants, and with which they have been content. A step-ladder, with a hand-rail, covered in red cloth, facilitates her operatioEs, when she cannot otherwise reach. Stephen, meanwhile, is idly leaning against the billiard- table in the centre of the saloon, with his hands in his pockets, his only occupation being to watch the operations of his companion, but one with which he seems perfectly content. - -
"Pray, sir, arn't you going to help me to put a soul into all this lifeless greenery?" she asks him. _
" How ? "
"Why, by flowers, which I am sure must be the souls oi plants made visible. Goodness gracious, Stephen, if air our souls were likewise made visible, I wonder how we should come off?"

" Ah, that would be a revelation for some of us!" 'Once more, are you going to help? Look at the lovely things waiting to shed their light and influence on the great world of society to-night through your handiwork! Look!" she said, showing her basket. "Really, I don't feel equal to so grand a vocation," was the response. "What then are you going to do ? " "Arouse myself in accordance with my humbler capacity." And therewith Stephen took a cuse and eh:liked the tip,while she ascended the st,p-ladder, and began to place the flowers. "All men, I suppose, have their ambition. And I have mine," added Stephen, as he rolled the balls on to the table, "And that is—?" "To make six sucsive ~and successful strokes off the spot. I did one day reach five., but generally my failures are humiliating. Here goes ! " but so did not the ball into the pocket when he struck. Miss Vandeleur, laughing, said, " I'm 80 glad—l mean so sorry. Try again." He does try, but though once more reaching five, he sf

fails; gets or ptetends to get a little angry, and explodes; to the great amusement of his companion, who ironically exhorts him to persevere, which he shows her by a look of humorous defiance is just what he means to do—and does, at intervals, through the subsequent dialogue. "Pray, young lady," says Stephen, pausing after another failure at the ignoble point of two, "do you know that my mother expressly forbade any pillage from the conserva- tory?" "No, I don't know, and just now I don't want to know. But be sure you tell me when I have quite done. Besides, I'm only robbing Peter to Day Paul l" "Did you ever submit to be Peter, and to be robbed ?"

44 Nf "I have. And as I find that Paul generally objects to being robbed in his turn, I too object on behalf of myself and the flowers." " Ah, but they are so charming! Look! Only look at these clusters of white and scarlet Bouvardias I have just put up," she said, standing on the top of the step-ladder. Stephen did look, and with interest, as he ejaculated— " Charming, indeed !" " Foolish fellow! I didn't ask you to look at me, but at these, these," she said with comic emphasis, as she tapped the flowers. "Can't I choose 2" "Certainly not !" "Perhaps you are right!" rejoined Stephen, with a half. sigh, or pretence at one. "I am always right; or, if not, I expect to be always thought so, which does equally well." And with a fresh burst of laughter she bade him go on with his failures, till she wanted him by-and-bye to count her successes. Stephen, it must be acknowledged, might well turn from the flowers to the face that was so near, and so bewitching in its present mood of abandonment to every impulse or passing thought. The mirthful, mischievous eyes, blue as the loveliest depths of a cerulean sky, and sparkling with new lustre at every hit she gave or received (whether real or fancied was much the same to -Frances); the cheeks radiant with colour that belonged even more to health than to beauty; the lips that seemed to play the part of a mocking antagonist even when they did not speak—all these, accompanied by that lovely, indefinable thing called expression, and revealing character, in her case a most at- tractive one superficially, if exceedingly faulty in deeper things, all these could not make Stephen forget her relations with the Earl, his brother, on the one hand, or withdrav his glance wiLhout an effort, when bh he so challenged him, on the other.

Stephen had indeed a manlr and winning form and face. He was not yet of age; tall, slender but strong, graceful alike in movement and rest. He had very light, long brown hair, a rich brown eye that at ordinary tunes seemed to revel now in joyous mirth, now in sarcastic observation, but at others was full of a strange, restless activity—a searching light as of inquiry, that might range through ' earth and heaven and still corns back dissatisfied. To Miss Vandeleur's eyes he was simply delightful, So bright was he, so apparently careless, prepared to take the rough and smooth of the world with an unchanging smile, as if it did not really matter which! A trifler, who yet managed somehow to make trifling respectable, and who had been known to say trifles were the only things in which he never trifled; a companion who was charming when he liked his company and chose to be so. Such were Miss Vandeleur's general impressions about her relative, and such was the average view of the persons among whom they moved. She did net know or suspect what his wandering eye might in some chance moment surely have warned her of, independently of other manifestations (that would, how- ever, only reach her in a modified form), namely, that there existed something deeper in Stephen apart from, pos- sibly antagonistic to all that she saw, even while that un- noticed something enhanced hy its effects her pleasure in his society. A sudden overcast of the face as if the actual shadow had passed between it and far-off light; an abrupt dissonant tone amid the harmonies of the most genial and jovial com- munion; an unexpected and curt refusal in some matter in which he had been confidently relied on, and no appar- ent cause or explanatien given to lessen the unpleasantness; were surely traits to stimulate the curiosity of a keen obser- ver and student of human nature. But Frances Vandeleur was no such person; and she had tie aid to accurate judg- ment from others, for Society took of Stephen in these things, if it ever noticed them, very much the same plea- , .L Such then was the hero of our story. Such the heroine, about whom we must add a few words explanatory of those relations with the Earl, which restrained Stephen in his in- timacy with his fair companion. Long years ago an unwritten compact had been made between the deceased Earl and the father of Frances Van- deleur that they would use their joint influence to secure her union with the Earl's eldest son and heir, when she shculd be old enough to marry. Her parents died within a few weeks of each other, and while she was still at school, but fast ripening into woman- hood. The Earl soon following, the widowed Countess brought the orphaned girl, then in her sixteenth year, to her own home, where she has ever since been. But the very first hour of Miss Vandeleur's residence in Harlaxton House the Countess with great delicacy referred to the engagement in order to say— " Think of it, my dear, as a matter that must be agree- able to us all, if what has been so long talked of comes to piss; but one in which you must and shall be free as air to choose." Miss Vandeleur blushed and was confused, but the Coun- tess could see her words had been a relief. And from that moment the young lady apparently considered that the best way to follow the Countess' advice as to how she should think of the matter was—not to think of it at all ! She was young, beautiful, rich, with all the world before her, and she was henceforth free! She had no objection to the Earl. She did not at all know that she might not at some time marry him. Suffi- cient for the day was the good thereof. She could have asked but one thing more from. Fortune—absolute freedom —and now she haeit ! And for her thenceforth, life, world, future, appeared wholly bright and inexhaustible. "Please mind your own huainess, and don't attend to mine! " Stephen is now saying to her. "Why ?'' "Because I have again got to number live and expect to get to number six." "If you were a true knight you would, for that very reason, ask me to look on to inspire and guide you to victory, and reward you with a wreath of glory after." "Come down, then, and I'll try. But don't speak—don" stir—don't breathe—don't —" "Live the while! I won't if I can help it. keep me long dead—it isn't nice." Slowly, deliberately poising his cue, measuring and re- measuring the imaginary line to the red ball on the spot, and from it to the Pocket, he struck, and before the ball had fairly reached its destination, he said, cooly— "l've done it ! " and he had. The ball rolled into the pocliet. She clapped her hands rejoicingly, and said, "If I were to hang a wreath round your head you would grow too vain and presumptuous, so I shall put this flower into your buttonhole instead." She took from her basket a Nehite' camellia only just opening, and placed it in his coat; Stephen looking his thanks rather too effectively, for while saying nothing he made her blush. "Well, now, Stephen, I do want your help to finish this jib," she continued, "by dotting at intcr, or camellias on the foliage along the coreiee, which I can't reach." "Send for the Earl, my brother. lie's taller than I, and will do anything to please you, even to growing amiable, if you don't keep him at it too long. Shall I seek him, or send for him?" " You lazy creature,.-No! I don't believe you care a bit for the glorious night we are going to have!" "Or for the fresh lovera that we expect to enrol in our train, eh ?" " What thou do you care for ?" " You are not my confessor." "Oh ! then you have something to confess? Well, never mind, I'm told we shall know about everything some day, and of that I suppose among the reel." " Perhaps." " Well, I'm going to tell you a secret." " Don't if I am to keep it a secret; the responsibility is too great," said Stephen. "Well, you must know there is a Fancy Bazaar getting up to benefit some charity ; I forget what, but a very good one." "Is that your secret?' "If you don't be quiet, and hear me out, I shall run away." " Might that not be too clanaerous a temptation?" " Will you, sir, be quiet ?" - "11l try." " Well, and there are such preparations! Half-a-dozen Countesees, who I verily believe never did a stitch of work in their lives, or saw a thimble, are said to be busy now with their needles. Mind, I don't vouch for the fact. And the stalls will be so beautiful, and the keepers of them so carefully selected—and oh, Stephen !—I am to be one, and have a stall all to myself." "And carry the principle and practice you have learned in the pillage of flowers into the larger field of humanity? Rob right and left, before and after, without scruple as with- out remorse ? " Reiterated bursts of merriment were Frances' only com- ments • and which Stephen could hardly help sharing, in spite of his grave face. " Well, now, Stephen, isn't that a secret worth listening. to ? "

While he was thas engaged, she also rapidly descended and going to him, said— " War itself recognises the beneficence of those who come under the banner of the Red Cross." "As displayed in your cheeks? " asked Stephen, forgetting his pain in the vivid beauty of the face before him. "Under that defence I come to help you. Let me look." He held out his hand, and she deftly drew the thorn forth, while he gazed at her, forgetting everything else in the world—excepting his claim, which he began to press. "Thanks! The issue is now changed. You owed me a debt. Now I owe you one. Cannot both be settled at the same time ?
