Then, remembering, perhaps, that discretion is the better part of valour, she tripped away, humming a popular nporatio air, lc.olzing laqolz at him all the white. CHAPTER X.—THE CABINET. Richards had not long left the Countess to fulfil his double duty, that relating to the invitations, and that of keeping the young people in ignorance, before he was again summoned to her presence. "I want the key of the closed room," she said abruptly. I have occasion to go there." Richards literally held up his hands in horror at the thought. "That room, your ladyship? Why, ic has never been opened since my lord, the Earl, died." "Surely no one should know that so well as I, who gave the order to close it !'' "But, my lady, it must be full of dust and cobwebs, and spiders and other nasty things. A dreadful place to go into! :But tc-morrow we can have it put to rights." "To-morrow !" echoed the Countess. And then in her heart, she added, "Will there be for me any sach to-mor- row ?" Moved probably by the picture of desolation he suggested, which had not occurred to her own pre-occupied mind, and which shocked her for quite different reasons than the physical uspleasantness, she said, after a brief pause— " Ivant some papers from the cabinet. Can I depend upon you to have it brought here the moment the men re- turn, untouched, except for the removal of the dust, if it be as you say ?" "It shall be here in a few minutes. I will myself open the door, do what needs to be done to the cabinet, not let it out of my iht, till under your ladyship's own eyes." "Thanks, my good Richards, that is just what I wish. Be as quick, then, as you can." He went out, but came back to say that both the foot- men in-waiting had returned, so that they would bring the cabinet at once. Though the Countess had changed her purpose to go to the room in question herself, she could not but follow in agitating thought those who were about to intrude on the lonely solitude of the chamber of death ; for it was not only there that her husband had died, but it was there that she had made known to him the perilous secret of her life; and after a brief but terrible period in which she had ex- pected he would carse her with his dying breath, he had melted in compassion, forgiven her, but held her bound by the most solemn... compact, to act as he laid down for her in writing; not merely " before her death," but before any imminent danger of death known to, or suspected by her. That paper, and others connected with it, are in the cabinet, about which she is so anxious, that she cannot but open her door to listen. She hears the bustle of the removal, and she hears the cabinet strike once, twice, against the wall, being heavy and unmanageable; and each blow seems to reverberate through her soul in her fear of any unforeseen accident tending to exposure. The burden approaches—is brought into the Countess's room by the two footmen, Richards carefully guarding it to the best of his ability by hand, and voice, in his directions to the others; but all the same' as the men bear it to a part of the room silently indicated by the finger of their mis- tress, it gets tilted and shaken as it reaches the floor, and a drawer that happens to be unlocked starts forth, and falls to the ground. With a cry of anger the Countess rushed to the place where the drawer lay, stooped to touch and glance at the contents, then turned from it, ashamed at the excitement and display, as she recognised their unimportant character. "There is no harm done, I see, James," said the Countess to the man, who stood gazing at her in helpless fear of the consequences of his slip. "That will do. Please Richards, mind what I said about my son." And then she was left alone with the cabinet; which soon filled for her the place where she was with shadows of the departed, that for the time became more real to her than could be any of those guests she had invited and for- bidden.

Suppose then yon tell me, say as a brother, just what you think of me." " But what if I don't think of you ?" " Pooh, that's nonsense. Now, will you do it ?" " No, indeed." "Why not ?" " Moths who are wise fear the candle." "Are you wise ?" "In that, yes. Perhaps in that only." " Well, at all events you must be wiser than me—l f 0 young." " And Iso old !" A simultaneous burst of laughter en- sued, which had the effect of thawing Stephen so far that he asked her— "ls it compliment you seek P" "No, the truth." 'A medicine which I must take care te make pleasant." "On the contra.) y, I challenge and defy .7411 to do your worst."

~.... worse than useless, a fruitful source of evil ; whilst compromising what she valued so highly, and held so sacred, her own honour, and the honour of her family. Did the thoughts occur in all their sinister significance,— I " I alone now live to be responsible for what was done. And I alone know." The reverie was abruptly broken. She took a larger en- velope to enclose the letter, sealed it with her own seal, and wrote a few words outside. Then hearing some one at the door, she hastily returned the letter to the jewel case, before the entrance of a servant announcing Mr. Lynx, the family solicitor. Short, thin, and wiry, bending as if he were engaged in a perpetual bow, which yet had no humility in it; but seemed only a convenient screen to veil the sharp, penetrating, distrustful glance, which his cold, steelly eye shot forth from time to time upon all with whom he was brought -into contact who might become hostile; no greater contrast could well be imagined that Mr. Lynx, and the Countess's ether professional adviser, Dr. Baxter. The Countess was his client: in bee:self and her family the most important of all his clients. She was a mourner, and full of that beagty which is so impressive because it is so Tare, the beauty of age when it is beautiful. These things Mr. Lynx was fully conscious of, and deferential geseordingly. But, nevertheless, there was an air about him which per- plexed the Countess. She did not like to stigmatise it in \her thoughts as suspicion—a prating himself on his guard —yet it looked so like that as to create a sense of annoy- ance; which revealed itself in the distant and haughty cold- ness of her tone and manner, as she began in the curtest words to give him directions. Curiously enough these unpleasantnesses, so far from affecting him unpleasantly, seemed, on the contrary, to re- store him at once to what might be supposed his normal equanimity, as she began— "l want a will preparing that shall bequeath everything I possess In my own right to my son Stephen. How long will it Wee you ?" "It has to be carefully drawn, revised by a conveyancer, fresh copies prepared; still, if time presses, it can be managed in three days." "It must be done in three hours!" "Quite impossible, your ladyship, if I am to stake my professional reputation on its sufficiency when done." "Then I must take another ronrae There are pens, ink, and paper. Please to write as I dictate." Mr. Lynx took his seat at the table and prepared to obey. The Countess began— "l, Mary, Countess of Harlaxton, widow of the deceased Earl of Harlaxton, give and bequeath my freehold house and estate of Southwell, in Gloucerershire, and all my personal property of every 'kind whatsoever to my son, Stephen--" "My second son," corrected the lawyer, looking up from under his grey, bushy eyebrows at the Countess; who saw the glance and was strangely affected. by it. "You confuse me. Please to write just as I give it to 1 you! He bowed in acquiesance, but that look had opened a new and more fearful vista to the Countess. Could the dying Earl have confided the secret of the Laver in the cabinet to his legal adviser, and concealed the fact from her? Her cheeks flamed at the thought, but she lost not a moment in questioning him. "Do you recognise this ? " she said, placing her hand on the jewel case before her. "Yes." "And this ? " She drew forth the letter, forgetting for the moment its new covering. He looked at it sharply from a little distance before answering— "No, unless it is under a fresh cover." She broke the seal, and removed the envelope. "Do you now recognise it ? " " Perfectly." "And the contents?" "Were made known to me by the Earl himself." The Countess smiled, and was silent for a little time. But it was such a smile as only appears on the human face in moments of bitterest trial; a kind of ironical acquiescence in the dealings of fate, however awful they may be. She was thinking what would have been her position if she could have been tempted even for the most unselfish of reasons to destrey the letter, and felt overwhelmed with shame and humiliation. "_enything more ? " she asked. "Yes, he authei ised and required me by letter to do whatever might be requisite, to see the things promised by your ladyship carried into effect; without, however, as I am bound and glad to say, expressing the slightest cloak of your fulfilling them, apart from any extraneous influ- ence." "That was very good of him! Very! Well, Mr. Lynx, there is one thing I can thank you for. You have been frank and straightforward with me; and the Countess of Harlaxton can ever be grateful for that. But since you know so much, let rne make an addition to your knowledge. Read what I had written on the new cover, the moment before you came in." The lawyer took the cover, and read— " For my beloved son, Stephen. Not to be opened, without my express permission, till after my death." "And this you intend to give to him ?" "The chamber where my husband died has been re- entered for the first time to-day in order to bring the cabinet here that I might be ready with this. I shall presently return,- it to the case, and to the secret drawer of the cabinet. And please to understand, once for all, there it will remain while I live, if not previously given to my son, or taken out to give him. And there you will find it when lam no more. I have two keys. Take one of them." All the lawyer's secret doubts and fears, with which he had come prejudiced, seeing how powerful were the temp- tations to eternal silence, now melted away like frost in the warm sun. is mintier changed. He became profoundly respectful, and ut/Wontedly sympathetic. Addressing himsAf first to the will the Countess had dictated, he finished it from where he had left off; gave it to her to sign; called in Richards and the Countess's maid to be witnesses; Lady Hariaxton acknowledged the signal hire, and dismissed them. Then the lawyer said to her, jestingly,— "The only objection I have to make to your ladyship's will is that it is so good you will be wanting no other." "Let this, then, be my will, while you prepare a more formal one. And this same jewel-case shall be its place of deposit, with my husband's letter and the other docu- ments." "And now, Lady Harla \ton, may I he permitted to say that I shall be proud to render you any service in my power." She looks at him long and wistfully. She did want some one to share her counsel ; and nowhere could she look for a better man, now that his true mind and feeling were vis- ible, and known to be friendly to herself. She made the venture: "Dr. Baxter warns me I am in danger. I may live many years, but meantime he finds it necessary, at my de- sire, to resort to strong measures even to secure me a single- day."

CHAPTER XII.—THE Finn. STEP. Seeing how ill the Countess looked, and noticing beside!. her great and peculiar agitation, Lord Harlaxton restrain the resentment seething within him, that his mother shoula. have countermanded all the invitations of the night withoag• even consulting him; and forgetting as he chose to think he did, that he and the young heiress could very well lase* fulfilled the duties of hospitality, even if she (the Countess) had been unable herself to share them, or even to be present. • It was clearly ne time for the display of temper OD that ground. And besides he had newer matters of c°l3l: plaint to be spoken of presently, when she had recoyereo herself. Taking her hand, as they met, he kissed her, hoped SO was better, and led her to her chair. She felt the coldness of his demeanour, and answered corresponding feeling. He had now taken a seat at the table, and was evideng unwilling to begin what he wanted to say, in the Counters state; so uttered a few words upon whatever subject uppermost, which she replied to with more iaterest 103' she had before shown. Her eyes being then directed towards him, she sat/ .kiir mechanically take up some paper from the table, and .10_""; at it; as men will in seeking trivial occupation that lit disguise their thoughts from those present, and who are may be watching. er it For an instant she did not see or think what paP--6-, was, till the change in the Earl's face told her the trn She had, in her hurry to conceal from him the all-inmorttill packet, and its place of deposit, forgotten the additiOav cover, and writing she had placed on it. Presently he looked up, and said to her, his handsolnel 4 common-place countenance flushing with renewed anger al:, excitement the while— ftdif " May I ask the meaning of this, which I find 00 table?" He then read aloud the inscription which' cated, the reader"will remember, that the packet was for rat Countess'" beloved son," but not to be opened, without '3* express permission, until she was dead. " Sir.ce it refers to Stephen and not to you, I do nottO you should ask." 110 "And the contents—which I see have flown—do they - refer to Stephen alone, and not to me ? " • "Do you presume to question me ? " ehOlf "Mother, I will tell you the truth. The favour you to my brother, and which he so ill repays, is becomicr subject of scandalous gossip." Pale as death, but perfectly collected, the Countess confronted him, to as in low tones, and slowly deliv,w:e words— "And what do they dare to say ?" "Oh, nothing that one can take hold of. And I 0"-40e not myself attach the slightest importance to their rea33o, but that Ido not—cannot any longer conceal from ittlkoeg you do not care for me as you do for my brother. -VOL,. things from me that, as your eldest son, and his brOu'iii b, have a right to know. I went out this morning to M/ Cioa expecting to meet at night all those whom we have soa-oat neglected, and I there learn you have reversed all,/,0 arrangements—nobody is to come! I return home hurt°4ool and I meet Mr. Lynx, who has had business witha.a."ge and a long interview, but who cannot find time to CIACP`-iyt half a dozen words with me, his principal emplol,efea. eis man meets me in the ball, and ask me to pay 0"-enel hundred and odd pounds thet Stephen has owed him know not how long, and threatens to arrest him beforetot very face if I refuse, which I certainly did. etnaetaer reminds me that I had been previously waylaid by say, of man—disreputable to the last degret, but a frieno ta Stephen's, so he told me—and asking me to guide h,hlote his friend! They did meet finally, and both insultepat I come to yen, and scarcely have we exchanged b''';os dozen words before some mysterious secret between Yoloeo my brother crops up, and then you wonder and take 0",,e sll if I say, as I do now—ln heaven's name, what does mean ?" The Countess was visibly moved. "Philip," she said, calling him by his Christian 0110,1 which she did so seldom that its recurrence always In!hr a mood of favour towards him, "there is much of trutract your complaint. I can say no more now, but I Wl' forget it. I have been—l am ill—very ill." "But can I be of no service in such a time 1, lawyer; cannot I —." She interrupted him to sot' ail! " The lawyer is drawing up my will; which as Yot' expect, and I hope approve, is entirely in faveg'„ a Stephen. Poor boy! He has nothing, and as nothing." "And will be nothing unless he very much Men- ways." beif then "Help him in that if you can! If you cannot, woe with him for a time for my sake. I own he seems friree —careless of eveything beyond the present hour; fear to indulgencies of which he ought to be asharo which he will be ashamed, bat whicn in my soul h,!datls spring mainly from his having no settled vocation; or to create ambition, if he has not already felt its spur; develope it in the pursuit of worthy and noble ends, tot already lives and stirs at times in his breast! 013 bjel me, Philip, he will emerge, and make us all proud yet; of those at least who may live to see." The Earl was now somewhat moved in his turn sirs" sorrowful meaning of these last words, and asked kindly interest— " Cannot something be done ? " Vid "My dear Philip, that is just what I am coming t°' must get him merged, and well merriel. Make bill/ politician, or courtry gentleman and magistrate, cultica;ll4 his own gardens and farm. Depend upon it a wife guide him the way he should go, if she is a true wile' really cares for him." "And where is that exemplary young lad 9 tO found ? " "Where, but at our own hearth ? " The Earl started to his feet in surprise and anger. be " What! Miss Vandeleur, to whom you and hr, knew I am paying my addresses? This is too much • " Philip, answer me. Has Miss Vandeleur yet Wren; Single word that can justify you in treating her as Y(440 peculiar property; or make it wrong in me, or in Ste` to wish him to try his chance ? " he let "I have no doubt of my success with her, if she alone!" "Can the Earl of Herlaxton be content with a saj,gbo gained through such ignoble conditions? Pardon word escaped. But I shall appeal to you on other grusit, Think what you have of the world's goods; what a Pc' 00f, you enjoy! And then think of Stephen's destitute Geo. tion, and join me in the work of building up his forteMtble "In any other way I will—cordially. But not Disallif I love Miss Vandeleur—l have proposed to her. 1113 I will submit to no interference there." "You really have proposed to her ?" "In effect, yes." "And her answer—? " aeft "Was what such answers often are, a check for the pt but no more." d The Countess rose from her seat, went to him, s° ,) his hand, while she said in tones of the deepest pattl7, tof "I cannot tell you, not now, all that is in my hOr'lll7 I entreat you—it is in all probability a dying mot h% ntAlb speaks—l entreat you to let me have my own wai 1,405 I conjure you to abandon all farther pursuit of this fst-to; lady till—till at least she can arrive at a knowledge own mind between you. You have had your elestav Stephen now have his." "You forget it was my father's wish that I shou Miss Vandeleur." "It was mine, too, in years long gone by." OsTa "You know how anxious he was that the Castle laxton, the cradle of our race, should be rebuilt, 0,041 deemed from its present disgraceful state. That is,"w with my present income: I can and shall do it, with Vandeleur's fortune." "The Castle can wait." "Pardon me, I think not." "It must!" tY " Must ?" "It must! It shall! Tempt me no more !' • Countess rose to her feet. "I stand upon my rights." i or "But be sure, Lord Harlaxton, that you do 00 ,a them. I now say my last word—beware !" tiSigyr She then turned her heck on him, and left lila-100;1' at his leisure the warning she had given, by abrut"- ing the room.

4 nrust you will incur no fresh risk." " You are too late ; I have acted. Let us hope an will be well, and use the time as if we anticipated the reverse. Listen." In low tones, but full of the deepest significance she said : " Wkat if Stephen were to mug Miss Vandeleur, my relative, the heiress; and with the IVealth she brings him, and what I can bequeath, becomes rich enough to found a new family, perhaps even obtain a new title ?" "Yes Pi "Surely you must know what else I woufoi say ?" "That your son might then be content to leave his rights in abeyance ?" "To sink them altogether for my sake, and for the yet unblemished honour of a noble family !" "But he knowing his rights, and in possession of every- thing necessary for his claim ?" "Most certainly." "That might be a desirable conclusion, but one that no man so situated ever consented to, or ever will consent to."

"But if he does consent ?" "Then there's an end of the matter, so far as he is con- cerned." "And I will look no farther." His words had given great relief to the Countess. She had feared that her husband in showing he would not trust her alone with the secret, or the fulfilment of her pledge to him, might have gone farther still, and left her no choice as to the ultimate solution, in which all her hopes were now confined. That difficulty was clearly out of her path. And the dis- covery became a new incentive to carry out her plan; one long since dimly shaped out; and so spare herself and family those revelations to the world, that grew more and more awful to her in contemplation. "Shall I surprise you, Mr. Lynx, if I ask you to prepare yet another document, also dealing with the disposal of all lam worth, apart from a life annuity of five hundred a year ?" "Nothing surprises a lawyer, even the not taking his ad- vice, provided you don't tell him so." "I should like a deed of settlement preparing to give my property to Stephen on his marriage with Miss Vandeleur. At present he has only a yearly allowance." "Ah yes, I understand! A. rough draft shall be ready, for you within two or three hours." "Can you entrust it to a safe man? One who will be silent, without even knowing it is necessary to be silent, seeing I may fail, and the marriage never take place?" "Let me consider. I think Ido know one safe and silent person who may be entrusted with the job. But your lady- ship knows him too, and may be dubious?" "Who can you mean ? " "Myself." The lawyer had been trying to win a smile. He suc- ceeded now. And said no more. The Countess held out her hand which he gasped so cordially as to pain her. But the pain itself was received as pleasure, betokening the strength of his feeling, and so they patted. The Countess was now left as she hoped and believed in possession of ample means to secure%the success of the scheme she had devised, and which the more she dwelt on, became only the more attractive. Suddenly there was a rush of blood to her head at the sound of a loud angry voice in the corridor i • which in an instant changed the character of her thoughts, and caused her to put hurriedly her husband's packet, and the newly- made will into the jewel case. But the case itself she had not time to place in the secret receptacle, so she thrust it into the drawer which had fallen out during the removal, and was invitingly half-open. She had scarcely done this and returned to her chair before the door opened, and Lord Harlaxton entered.

div.p: MARRIA.GE OF DR, McDOUGAIL. OF

RUNCORN, The marriage of Dr. Finlay McDougall, of Runcorn, with Miss Alice Willis, youngest daughter of the late Mr. Frederic Willis, solicitor, of Leighton Buzzard, took place in All Saints' Church, Leighton Buzzard, on Thursday morning. A very large concourse of people congregated within the grand old edifice and in its precincts to testify to the general interest manifested in the wedding. The weather in the morning was dull, but as the day advanced the clouds broke away, and all fears that the sun would not shine upon the bride were dissipated. The assembly in- cluded persons of all ages and both sexes drawn from all grades of society in the town, but, as usual on such an in- teresting ard important occasion, the ladies were most numerously represented. The ceremony was fixed to. take place at half-past eleveg, and for nearly an hour previous to that time the carriages conveying the bridal patty from the residence of Mrs. Wiilis in liockliffe-read were

hurrying to and from the church. The newly restored and beautiful chancel was very nicely decorated for the occasion with choice flowers, specially supplied by Mr. Hamlin, of the Bletahley Park Nurseries. Mrs. Hamilton presided at the organ, and as the wedding party entered the church played Batiste's Adante in G. The bride was attired in a very rich broche satin dress, spotted tulle veil, and hair and dress. decorations of natural flowers. She wore also a massive gold necklet and locket., set with diamonas, this being the. gift of the bridegroom, as was also the large and beau:Hal bouquet of stephanotis, orange blossoms, and other choice flowers she carried. There were four attendant Insides- maids—namely, Miss Mabel David (neice of the bride), Miss Alice Archer (cousin of the bride), Miss Rigdea, and Miss Florence Senior. These ladies wore dresses of cream Indian muslin, profusely trimmed with lace; tartan sashes of the bridegroom's clan; Henri 11. hats, trimmed with heather, cream satin, and lace, and lined with ruby velvet. Their silver brooches, of novel design, set with cairngorms and Scotch pebbles, were the gifts of the bridegreona. The bridesmaids carried bouquets of choice dowers. Mr. Ross ee was the bridegroom's "best man." The bride was led to i is. the altar and given away by her brother, Mr. G.orbe Willi The ceremony was performed by the Rev. div.head: CHAPTER XL-THE DAWNING PLAN.
div.p: CHAPTER XL-THE DAWNING PLAN.

Presently the opened the zabinet, took from It a number of written documents, and began to destroy them after a glance at their contents, by tearing them into piecas, and throwing them on the fire. The process distressed and wearied her; and led to the question—Could she afford time for such labour how? She stopped, returned the unexamined papers to the cabinet, unlocked a secret drawer, and took frcm it a small red morocco jewel case, which she placed on the table; while she sank into her chair to let the physical agitation caused by the act pass away Then she opened it, drew forth a letter, and read the in- scription, on the back:—
To TUB
HON. STEPHEN C. FEMME,

murmuring the while— 'oh, Stephen,-Stephen, what wilt thou say when thou shalt know by this message from thy dead father, thou art his true heir, the rightful Lord of Harlaxton ?" She did not attempt to read the letter, which had been left unsealed. Its contents-were only too well known to her. But she held it in her hands a long time. Did the temptation occur u her to destroy the letter, as she had destroyed those other tiseless and uncompromisinp papers? Did she ask herself whether indeed this packet might not

_ WHERE ARE THE POLICE? I Sir —I think it would be well if the "Great Unpaid" directed the attention of the Chief Constable to the some- ' what unseemly conduct of the young men and maidens who frequent Sankey-street on the Sunday evenings. No sooner is the service concluded at our various places of worship than the thoroughfare is thronged with yoang persons 1 whose behaviour is only fitted to a fair ground, and even 1 there it would be discreditable. Not only is the jostling 1 from oneiAde of the street to the other very annoying, but 1 the loud laugh and the profane language which frequently greets the ear are most offensive. It is utterly impossible for sober-minded people to wend their way along in com- fort. If the Chief Constable would not only have two or three subordinates stationed at the corners of the thorough- fare, but would also see that others are posted at short dis- tances frorneach other along the whole length of the street; and if, moreover, one or two of the "young gentlemen and ladies" were "run in," I venture to think there would soon te an improvement.l am, la., PASSER-BY. Warrington, August, 1883.

div.head: POLITICAL ORGANISATION IN RUNCORN.
div.p: POLITICAL ORGANISATION IN RUNCORN.

6ir,—Having recently been on a visit to Runcorn, and having made a few observations as to the state of political organisation there, may I request the favour of a little space in your columns for the publication thereof, and for the discussion of the beet means 'whereby to improve it and the town generally. Entering into conversation with a friend of mine I chaflingly remarked that the Runcorn dis- trict must be a highly Tory district thet it could not return a Liberal to ParliaMent at the last eleet!on for Mid-Che- shire. " Why," w s the reply, " how can you eXpect any- thing else, when there is no interest taken in p9liticAl Matters except at election times ? Between elections one never hears politics mentioned; or, if they are, it is only I in a half-hearted, timid way ; the person who introduces the subject being looked upon ae ft disturber of the company, and the sooner got rid of the batter." The town possesses no news rooms, no political associations. It possesses no or- ganised staff of workers for critical political occasions. It does possess numerous pubic-houses and drinking vaulte, but I only saw about three newsagents shops, and one so- called workmen's club. Let us hope that that is doing good work. Now, many of the older parts of the town con- sist of houses with rooms so small and uncomfortable that it it almost unna' ural to expect men after a hard day's work to remain in them long at a time. Dark, dingy, with unhealthy smells, too small for a family of two—not to speak of the larger families that are common in England, the men have no alternative but to seek some more con- genial retreat. What more natural than that they should rush from that extreme to the other, the brilliance of the well-lighted vaults and taverns, in the absence of more suitable places of resort. And it is a well-known fact, to anyone who in the least observes these matters, that ' drinking does not conduce to the promotion of a population politically, morally, or physically. Could there not be something done to alter this state of things ? With this purpose in view could not there be a "Liberal Association" formed for the purpose of attending to all political matters in Runcorn by renting a room—not necessarily very large at first, but large enough to be pleasant, and airy enough for people to pass some time in it—and by paying a sub- scription of about ss. per year per member a news room, well supplied with papers and provided with such amusemen!s as drafts, dominoes, tè., could be maintained. This woul,i form a good centre for political organisation not only for Runcorn, but would extend some influence to the surround- ing districts. Such matters as registration', &c., could be attended to in the interests of the party, and a properly- organised staff of canvassers could be kept up in connection with the association. From the same centre also the poli- tical education of the people could be advanced by putting the association in connection with the National Reform Association, the Cobden Club, the Peace Society, or any et'sier of the greatand Liberal societies, and thus procuring lecturers to come and forward the political education frcm time to time. This would give the local gentlemen who at cite- tin times show so much activity an opportunity of mixing With the working classes and working with them for one ccohmmhen end, so that when the next opportunity comes Mid- es , ire may be prepared to do its p,rt in helping on th, reforms so much needed throughout the country, but more especially in the rural and agricultural districts. It would also tend to the raising of the moral standard of the town, to the intellectual dvelopment of the people, to increased habits of sobriety, and in fact to the general welfare of tip, inhabitants. Hoping that in the interests of a large popu- lation this matter may not be allowed to rest until another election is upon you, but that immediate action may be the result of this letter, allow me to subscribe myself Rochdale, August, 1883. A ROORDA.Lh VISITOR.

J's ALTRINCHAM. CHALLENGING TILE Intsu TO FlGHT.—Thomas Gannon was charged at Altriocham, en Tuesday, with unlawfully Wounding Thomas Winstanley, farm labourer, of Hale. The Pro2ecntor and other men went to the farm ..nd rhallpngad the Irishmen to fight. The defendant went out and struck %gar:tautly across the face with a heavy stick, cutting his lip and breaking some of his teeth. The bench, con,idering the provocation, fined the defendant only 203. and costs. .A.LTRINCHA.3I BUEWSTER SESSIONS —Tl,e annual licens- ff 2e5910n5 were held on Monday; Mr. T. W. Tatton, wythenshawe, presidin,. superintendent Leighton re- Ported that there were 13 licensed victuallers, 27 beerhouse keepers, and 42 grocers and others licensed to sell beer off 'lie premises in the Altrincham district, makin a total of 82, one licensed house to 135 of the inhabitants ; at Lymm 111 licensed victuallers, six beerhouse keepers, and seven out- door beersellers, or one licensed house to 186 of the inhabi- tants; Sale, five licensed victuallers, nine beerhouse keepers, pd 31 outdoor beersellers, or one to 255 of the inhabitants. In the whole district there are 57 licensed victuallers, 51 eersellers, and 91 outdoor beersellers, a total of 199, or one licensed house to 203 of the population. During the year 241 persons have been proceeded against for drunkenness, as Isainst 324 last year, thus showing a decrease of 83.—A deputation attended the court, headed by the Rev. Frederick Wainwright, vicar of St. John's Church, Altrincham, who Inbinitted a memorial, signed by over 500 persons, paying ttbe Bench not to grant any more licenses, and to curtail so /r as possible those existing.—The Chairman said the (Inch felt the great responsibllity of dealing with the trans- fer and granting of licenses, and the representations of the deputation should have due consideratiou.—Mr. Leresche, tarrister, applied on behalf of Mr. Witty, the proprietor of the Sale Botanical Hotel and tiardens, for an extension of the license to the ballroom and bowling green. The appli- cation was refused.—The Bench delined to renew the license of Jonas Rowbotham, the Plough Hotel, Ashton-on- etacY, and also those of William Minshnll, beerhonse • Timperley, and Edward Leather, beerhonse keeper, oale. A number of applications to sell beer on the premises ware refused, and the consideration of a number of transfers Was adjourned for the purpese of ascertaining whether they were necessary for the public convenience. BURTON WOOD. , BunToslwooD PUBLICAN FINED.—At the Newton ttY Sessions, on Saturday last, William Houghton, a pub- lican_, at Burtonwood, was summoned for selling whiskey aolulterated with water to an extent more than that allowed by the Act.—He pleaded guilty.—Superintendent Jackson stated that he sent a sample of the whiskey to Dr. J. Campbell Brown, of Liverpool, the County Analyst, who had certified that the whiskey was 33 degrees under proof, being 8 per cent. weaker than the utmost limit allowed by the Act.—The defendant war fined 20s. and costs. He found Taylor in the kitchen.—Ml. xon, for the defence, contended that Brown was not on licensed premises and that Taylor went to inquire about tine hay that had to be cut the following morning. Mr. Dixon called the landlord and his wife and they corrober- ated his statements.—The Bench dismissed all three cases beriev • ing that Brown was not on licensed premises and that Taylor was there bra lawful purpose. FRODSHAM VOLU)rTEERS.—By the kind invitation of Mr. James Reynolds, the I Company (Frodshatn) of the Earl of Chester's Rifled held their annual sham fight at Fox Hill, on Saturday evening. The company paraded at the Town Hall at rive o'clock, under the command of Cap- tain Ashton and Lieutenants Henry and Harrison, and each man was supplied with 30 rounds of ammunition. They then wont, accompanied by the band, direct to Fox Hill Head, where at six o'clock they were divided into two com- panies. One, under the command of Lieut. Harrison, was sent to defend the tower situate on Fox Hill; the attacking party being under Captain Ashton. Lieut. Harrison placed his men in good positions to defend the tower; but by the skill of Captain Ashton the men under his command soon carried the height amid cheers. During the manoeuvres Colonel Ashton and Captain Kerr (the Cheshire Regiment, adjutant of the Earl of Chester's Rifles) acted as umpires. The men were afterwards entertained by Mr. Reynolds, and at the conclusion of the feast the call of Captain Ashton for three cheers for Mr. and Mrs. Reynolds was heartily re- sponded to, the band playing " For he's a jolly good fel- low." The men then marched home. On Sunday the com- pany paraded for Divine service in the Parish Church, and there was a good muster. The Battalion Challenge Cup net having been competed for during the camp, each company will be tried on its own ground. VALEDICTORY SERMON OF REV. J. M. BAMFORD, AND FAREWELL MEETING.—On Sunday evening, the ktev. J. M. Bamford delivered a valedictory sermon in the Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, which was attentively listened to by a large congregation, and on Tuesday evening a farewell tea took place in the school-room—which had been tastefully decorated with plants and flowers—when about 200 sat down. After tea a public meeting was held in the chapel, which was largely attended, and the Rev. F. F. Edmonds having engaged in prayer, Mr. Moss, of Helsby, senior circuit steward, was called to the chair.—The Chairman gave a short address, and the Rev. J. M. Bamford afterwards, in an excellent speech of half an hour's duration, gave a retrospec- tive account of his experience in Methodism, during which the rev, gentleman stated that his appointment to the Cheshire circuit was his eighth meve.—The Rev. F. F. Edmonds presented, on behalf of the friends in the circuit, a handsome marble timepiece, biscuit jar, and card basket, valua about £2O, and Mr. Bamford, on behalf of himself and wife, acknowledged the gift in suitable terms.—The meeting was then addressed by Mr. Turner, junior circuit steward, Mr. Proud, Mr. Walker Mr. Rimmer. and Mr. S. Smith, sen.—The choir gave a selection of music at inter- vals, and a pleasant feeling pervaded throughout the whole meeting, Mr. Bamford's speech being very cordially received, and bore abundant testimony to the success which has attended Mi. Bamford's earnest ministrations in the Frod- sham circuit. BRUTAL OUTRAGE ON AN IRISH HARVESTMAN—At Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, Stephen Oakes, Joseph Oakes, and Thomas Gayter, English labourers, were charged with having assaulted an Irish harvestman named chael Flannery, at Frodsham, on the 6th inst. Prosecutor was employed by a farmer named Percival, living near Frodsham, and on the day named he went into that village to purchase provisions. He came out of a shop in company with two other Irishmen and met the three prisoners, who asked him and his companions if they wanted to fight. Flannery haying looked around, Stephen Oakes asiired him what he was looking for, and without waiting for a reply dealt him a heavy blow on the left eye, which knocked him down. When he got up Oakes struck him again. They then struggled and fell together, Flannery being uppermost. Me got up and walleed away, but Oakes followed him, and then the two other prisoners came up and joined in the affray. Joseph Oakes got behind Flannery and pinioned his arms, while the other men hit him as hard as they could in the face for about five minutes. Gayter also kicked him when he was down. Flannery's clothes were torn, and his shirt nearly stripped off his back. He retreated with his two Irish companions into Mr. Davies's yard, but the Prisoners followed, and stoned him with macadam and paving stones. Prosecutor's face was terribly cut up, and his body bruised and injured. Mr. Davies then interfered, and drove the prisoners off with a sheep dog. The prisoners produced a belt with which they say the prose- cutor had assaulted them, but the prosecutor said he merely waved it round his head to keep the prisoners off. The prisoners were sentenced to a month's imprisonment each with hard labour. IRLAM AND CADISHEAD.

MANCHESTER CORPORATION AND WATER SUPPLY OP Ira„Am AND CA.DISHEAD. - At a meeting of the Barton Rural Sanitary Authority, on Wednesday, a deputation at- tended with respect to the supply of town's water to Irlam and Cadishead. They handed in a resolution passed by the Manchester Water Works Committee, stating that provided the above authority would guarantee the annual payment of £lOO, in addition to the guarantee of £2OO offered by the owners of property, and a sum of £l6B receivable from parties who will take town's water, the committee will lay the mains necessary for the supply of town's water to Irlam and Cadishead. A committee was appointed to draw up an agreement and wait upon the Corporation. SNUTSFORD.

DARING LEAP FROM TELAIN.—A daring leap from a train occurred on the Cheshire Lines nailwav on Saturday afternoon. Robert Wilkinson, a rag and bone gatherer, of Stockport, was being conveyed to Kiiutsroid in custody or an officer of the county police, he having been committed on a charge of theft to the ensuing sessions at that place. The officer and his prisoner rode in a first-class compartment, and when between AteLley and Mobberley Stations, while the train was going at full speed. Wilkinson made a clear dive head-foremost through the open window, and was seen spinning along for some distance by the side of the train. When the train slackened near Mobberlev the officer jumped out, and in doing so fell and hurt his ;boulder. He, how- ever, was not incapacitated, and, on proceeding to the place where his prisoner had escaped, easily succeeded in tracking him through the fields and recapturing hint. Strange to say, the prisoner was uninjured, save a slight scratch on his face.

INLAND linvENtTE.—ln the recent contest for eight studentships in the Labratcry of Somerset House, at South Kensington, which is confined to assistants of the Inland Revenue, and extends over a period of two years, we notice Mr. Henry Vivian Buckley, late of the Academy, Winsford, stood at the head of the list of the successful competitors, and will, therefore, shortly proceed to London. ANNITERSART.—The members of the Sons of Temperance, "Happy Family" Division, held their anniversary last Saturday. They walked through the streets, headed by the band of the Rifle Volunteers, and members carrying a splendid banner. They called at Fern Villa, the residence of R. Stubbs, Esq., where the band played a selection of music on the lawn. Tea was provided in the Primitive schoolroom, High-street, after which a meeting was held, over which Dr. Hector Leake presided. WINSFORD AND SANDBACH CIRCUIT —A new Free Methodist Chapel was opened on Monday last, at the ancicat town of Middlewich. The opening hymn," Before Jr,bovah's awful throne," &c., having been sung and prayer offered by Mr. John Buckley, F.R.G.S., the remainder of the service was conducted by the Rev. John Guttridge, of Manchester, whose sermon from let Kings, Bth chapter, and 27th verse, was most appropriate. The chapel was well filled. After the collection tea was provided in the Wesleyan school-room, kindly lent for .the occasion, when the tables were twice filled. After tea Mr. Guttridge delivered his popular lecture (under the chairmanship of George Slater, r.eq.), entitled "The Bible tested and triumphant," in which he was frequently stopped by rounds of applause. After each service collections were taken, and these, with the tea meet- ing, cleared about £3O. It is very pleasing to record that during the months in which the building has been in course of erection no accident has °purred% and now that it is finished we may safely say there is not a public structure in the town which surpasses it in appearance. Its capacity was well tested on Monday night. when not fewer than 350 attended the lecture. Votes to lecturer, chairman, givers of tables, and tea makers, as well as to the Wesleyan trustees f- the use of the school-room,were passed, and the first ser-

/The Chester city magistrates, on Saturday, took a new departure by refusing to grant permission to licensed vic- tuallers to sell intoxicating drinks on the Roodee on the occasion of the autumn sports. . CHESHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.—In consequence of a serious outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in the neigh- bourhood of Crewe, it has been resolved, at a meeting of the Cheshire Agricultural Society, to abandon the show of cattle, sheep, and pigs this year, and to hold merely a one day's exhibition of horses, turnouts, cheese, butter, poultry, and dogs. HonsE Fein AT CREWE.—The first horse fair prompted by the Crewe Cattle Market and Abattoir Company was held on Tuesday at Crewe. There was a fair show of heavy horses and ponies; but light horses were scarce. Buyers came from all parts of the district, and there was a good demand. Heavy horses fetched about £35 each; light horses, £2O to £3O; ponies, £lO and upwards. THE DUKE OF WESTMINSTER AT CHESTER.—The Duke of Westminster, who was accompanied by the Duchess, on Monday opened the Grosvenor St. John's National School at Chester, a handsome building, which has been erected at a cost of about £7,000, through the generosity of his grace. The building accommodates 400 children, and is well calcu- lated to meet the educational wants of the district. CHESHIRE, SHROPSHIRE, AND NORTH WALES FARMERS' ASSOCIATION—The annual general meeting of the members of this Association was held at Crewe on Tuesday; Mr. G. W. Latham, of Bradwell Hall, Sandbacb, presiding. The twelfth annual report recorded the continued progress of the Association. The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report, said they had done a thoroughly good business during the year. They had traded largely and successfully. He was glad to congratulate them on the improvement in the weather, and he hoped better days were in store for agri- culturists. If the beautiful weather continued they would be able to (get fairly average crops, in a thoroughly good state of preservation. He hoped, further, that after they had got in their crops they would have a dry autumn, so that they coeld clean land which had got dreadfully foul during the last two or three years. (Hear, hear.) The report and balance sheet were adopted, and the usual officers elected.

THE REV. J. YONGE ON THE LATE DR. MOFFAT- A large congregation attended the evening service at Weirsliffe Congregational Church, Warrington, on Sunday last, when the pastor (the Rev. John Yonge) preached a sermon to young men, "In memory of the late Robert Stotler, the apostle of Seutla Africa, who read his Tien to his life work on a placard near Warrington Bridge veventy years ago." Taking for his text the words, "To me to live is Christ" (Philippians i, 21.), the rev, gentle- man, in the course of his remarks, said those words of Paul he put before them as an explanation of Robert Moffat. They explained his life of devotion to paissionary labour, his life of heroic endurance, his life of unstinted and un- wearying service. Christ was Moffat's ideal, which he largely embodied in his life by steadfast purpose and quenchless enthusiasm. Proceeding to sketch Moffat's history, the preacher said he developed a great love of flowers and studied botany and horticulture, becoming at the age of 14 apprentice to a gardener. At the end of his term he gained a situation in the gardens of the Earl of Moray, where, however, he did not remain very long. Another situation was offered him which brought bias southwards into our own immediate neighbourhood, from which event the town of Warrington found so con- spicuous a place in the decisive accidents of his c .raer. He wished time allowed a detailed reference to the exiraience through which Moffat's obedience to his mothere"="desire that he should read a chapter of the Bible every day, led him at High Legh. He literally fulfilled her wish, although for long it was an obedience to the letter only, and the only pleasure he deriveci, was the sense that he was doing her will. BriW presently he became unhappy, and struggles took place in his soul. The truth was forcing its way to his conscience, and he longed for peace as sailors tempest driven longed for a haven. At length one evening, in his lonely lodge in the gardens of High Legh, while poring over the epistle to the Romans, new light streamed forth. The familiar words -seemed full of new meaning. "Turning from one passage to another, each sending a renovation of light into my alarkened soul, the Book of God, the precious undying Bible seemed to be laid open, and I saw at once what God had 'done for the sinner, and what was required of the sinner to obtain the Divine favour and the assurance of eternal life. I felt that being justified by faith I had peace I with God through our Lord Jessie Christ." "I had under- gone," he added, "a great change of heart, and this I be- lieve was produced by the spirit of God through -reading the Bible, and the Bible only, for my small stock of books consisted chiefly of works on gardening and botany." How truly could Moffat say "The entrance of Thy word giveth light: it giveth understanding to the simple!" What interest gathered around that gardener's cottage at High Legh, as they thought how the destinies of hundreds and thousands of those uncivilised and barbarous people "sitting in darkness and the shadow of death" were in that humble dwelling being eternally affected! Some years ago Moffat visited the spot in company with some Warrington gentlemen and as his eye rested upon his early home he burst into a flood of tears, and said "This is the vary place where God first met my soul." The house was still standing, and he (Mr. Yonge) cordially endorsed the luggestione which had reached him, that it would be well if the Congregational- ists in Warrington and neighbourhood erected a tablet on that house to Moffat's memory, bearing perhaps as a suit- able motto Paul's words, "To me to live is Christ," and also Moffat's own touching exclamation—" This is the very spot where God first met my soul." It was interesting to note, and it was a fine indication of his special fitness for his future work, that no sooner was Moffat converted to God than he began "to try to convince others of the necessity of repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ." That was a mark of the true missionary. He found a mission ever at hand, and needed not to wait to begin his labour until some specific sphere was assigned to him. From first to last there was nothing of the professional missionary about Moffat. In his hands Christ's Gospel never sank into a profession. It was his life work from the hour when first he saw the Lord. And new they found a striking illustration of how trifling a thing, how trifling an accident sometimes brought on a great crisis, and decided limitless issues. Daring his residence at High Legh, Mof- fat found that he wanted a trifling article which was not to be obtained nearer than Warrington. On a calm, beauti- ful summer's evening he walked towards our town. As he walked he thought. "I was imperceptively led to a train of thinking of the past—how much of my life I had spent serving the world, and not for Him who died for me." He resolved that in the future he would devote himself more completely to his Saviourerglory. As his position at High Legh was likely soon to be improved he dwelt with gladness upon the increased opportunities and powers he would have for serving Christ. Such were his thoughts as he entered the town and passed over the bridge. Somewhere near the bridge his eye was arrested by a placard en the wall. It was a missionary placard—the first he had ever seen. It announced a missionary meeting, at which the Rev. Virm. Roby, of Manchester, would take the chair. Moffat read and reread the bill as though irresistibly spell-bound and fastened to the spot. The date of the meeting had passed some weeks; but he could not withdraw his eyes from the placard. The sight of it brought back to his memory long forgotten tales of mission work in Greenland and Lebra- dor, told him in his boyhood by his mother, and a great tumult arose in his mind. He hurried away up town and bought the thing which he needed, and hurried back to the placard, read it again, and, said he, "Now I wended my way solitary homewards another man, or rather with another heart." He then and there resolved to be a missionary, and if he could find his way to the mission field nohow else he would " go to sea and get landed on some island or foreign ashore, where I might teach the poor heathen to know the Saviour." And so by the " accident "of a placard, and an old placard near Warrington Bridge, Robert Moffat found his call to his life work. "How great a matter a little fire kindleth !" If the fuel be but ready and sensitive a spark could do widespread work. Moff it's heart was already prepared. The soul in him was already sensi- tive to divine love and divine claim upon his service; and hence this trifle, this accident, was enough to determine his course and to divert him for ever from the culture of the garden to that of the wilderness, from the study of God's handiwork in the realm of flowers to the rescue of God's bandiwotk [rem its ruin in the realms of savage and un- civilised humanity. How beautifully true it became of this young gardener that, in his future life, " the wilderness and the solitary place were glad for him and the desert rejoiced and blossomed as the rose." At this time Moffat appeared to have wOrshipped with the Wesleyan Methodists, no Presbyterian or Congregational worship being at all con- venient. The Wesleyan Conference being then in session in Manchester, he and a companion went and stayed there some days. During this time he heard Mr. Roby preach, and was much impressed by his discourse. The lady of the house where he lived told him that night that Mr. Roby was "a great missionary MAN and sometimes sent out young men to the heathen." That remark decided Moffat to see Mr. Roby. which with marvellous bashfulness and fearful- ness he did next morning. Mr. Roby gave him encourage- ment, and after some brief delays, during which the directors of the society hesitated not a little as to whether he was fit to send out, Moffat was accepted as a missionary, and placed under Mr. Roby's care for a brief period of instruction. He seemed to have held a situation at Dukinfield while he was pursuing study under Mr. Roby's direction, and hence it was evident that he had none of those advantages which missionary students in these days considered essential and indispensable. Dukinfield, however, provided him with one advantage, the value of which he proved during half a century of life in Africa—it furnished him with a wife whose missionary zeal and Christian devotedness equalled and stimulated his own. In October, 1816, at Surrey Chapel, London, two celebrated men received together ordination to mission work in foreign lands—John Williams and Robert Moffat—the one finding an early translation to heaven in a' martyr's death, the other living for nearly 70 years to testify the gospel of the grace of God; and both leaving names on the Church's annals that will never be forgotten. Passing under review a career of upwards of 50 years of faith, courage, unselfishness, perseverance, and success, Mr. Yonge said Moffatreachei the Cape at the end of the year 1816, and was stopped from going to the native tribes by the Colonial Governor, who forbade him to cross the frontier. It was believed that his mission would do far more harm than good. But he was not to be de- feated. After some months' delay he found his way in spite of countless dissuading entreaties and gloomiest as- surances of defeat in his mission, and even loss of his life, to the kraal of Africaner, a Hottentot chief, who had become the dread of all the country round. However, this man, whom both civilized and uncivilized dreaded, whom they ' could neither bumble nor conquer, fell captive to Jesus Christ, and had left a name in Africa as beautiful for good- ness and grace as once it was infamous for cruelty and bloodshed. So did Moffat, even in his early mission, prove therreaptiveness of Christ's Gospel to the needs of man. After his marriage at Capetown to the young lady he found at Dukinfield, which occurred after he had spent more than three years as a solitary missionary among the tribe of Aft leaner, Moffat settled down in 1821 at Kuruman, among the people known as the Bechuanas, a tribe of infidels. The preacher then alluded to the difficulties Moffat experienced, s and to his translation of the scriptures in the native lan- guage for which he bad to invent a written form. When Moffat returned home in 1870 what was his statement as to the results of his half century of labour? This: "The Bechuanas, extending to 20 degrees south latitude, and all the other tribes, are open to the sound of the Gospel, and we see the messengers of the church proclaiming the Gospel to thousands and tens of thousands among them, who not long ago lived in gross darkness and ignorance. In the early days of my labour there was not one person who could read; now thousands of men, women and children among the Bechuanas are reading the Scriptures and books in their own tongue. I know that for years not one among tbem could be made to comprehend that a book or a paper could speak. The Gospel and Christian missions have done it all." As for Kurnman, the settlement created by Moffat himself, it was, and had long been, a bright oasis in the vast wilds of Africa. Its gardens and vineyards refreshed the travellers who passed that region, its church and schools, its printing office, and work- shops, and dwellings, were all so many results of Moffat's wprk, and so many forms of the civilising power of the Gospel. European manufactures to the value of £lOO,OOO a year were exchanged among the natives, and the country was safe for travellers among all the tribes. Moffat died at .Leigh, in Kent, on August 9th, aged 88 years. UP to the very last his energies were given eo the cause he bad loved and,

served so leng. Letters to a friend in Warrington, which be (Mr. Yonge) had been privileged to see, showed the old love unabated and the old faith undimmed. Africa was ever in his heart. It grieved him that sad and sanguinary strifes should have intervened, and that a misguided policy' bad done such mischief among the natives. It bad been alleged that he favoured the policy of Sir Bartle Frere, which led to the Zulu war. Those letters which he (the preacher) had seen, contradicted that notion. While respecting that statesman, Moffat believed his South African policy ruinous. To the last Moffat prayed and worked for Africa, arid only laid down his labour when the Master said, "Come up higher." Now he rested. Devout men carried his once stalwart frame to the tomb the other day, and laid his body beside that of his wife, who preceded him to the land of rest 12 years before. They did not make great lamentation. How could they ? Not premature his death. Not the mournful finish of a wasted life, his death. Not on any account a cause for sorrow or regret. "They glorified God in him," and they felt as he (Mr. Yunge) would that those present should feel that night, the wondrous influence of his life taking fresh possession of their hearts. He rested in the presence of his God, in the company of the redeemed, joining surely "the glorious company of the Apostles," and recognising here and there in the mighty multitude from all nations before the throne the glorified Africaner from Nemagnaland, and Klorified Bechuanos washed in the blood of the Lamb, who once owned no God, and knew of no heaven. Who could tell the raptures and delights that had already thrilled his soul, who could conjecture the many trophies he had laid at his Master's feet!

Se vant of God! Well done! Rest from shy loved employ; The battle fought, the victory won. Enter thy Maater's joy: S 'ldler of Ohrist ! Well d ! ! Praise be thy new employ. And while eternal ages run. Rest in thy Saviour's joy. One word more. It must be added. Moffat spoke to them that night from his place in yonder heaven. His heart cared for the countless tribes in the land of his adoption. And so it could not be difficult to phrase the message which he would send them from the skies. To every Christian he would say "live Christ more than ever, make Christ your ideal and pourtray list life in yours. Seek to make your Saviour known whatever be your lot in life." And to Christian young men the venerable and sainted hero seemed to address an especial word. He asked and called them to take up the work which be at length had laid down. Re- membering his own call on the placard by Warrington Bridge, he thought the departed missionary would appeal to Warrington youths in Wycliffe Church that night. and ask that some, that one at least, should volunteer for Africa. Which of them was willing to consecrate his service that day unto the Lord? Did it not seem as if to Moffat's voice another and diviner voice were joined, saying "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us ? " The question awaited its answer. Should it pass unheeded, unresponded to? Was there none who dare accept the challenge? Be it Africa or India, or China, or the islands of the sea, be it the land of their birth itself, there was room for them, and need for them; and a divine claim upon them. Surely the mantle of Elijah would fall upon some Elisha, and one should in his heart say to the Lord that night, "Here am I, Lord, send me."

div.head: WARRINGTON SWIMMING CLUB GALA.
div.p: WARRINGTON SWIMMING CLUB GALA.

It is doubtful whether there have ever been crowded into the first class plunge bath of the Warrington Corporation so many persons as there were on Thursday evening, on the occasion of the second annual gala in connection with the Warrington Swimming Club. The attendance was a great improvement upon that at the previous gala, and it was pleasing to notice that the greater portion of the spectators were adolescents, who were likely to derive much instruc- tion and ultimate benefit from the natatory exhibitions which they witnessed. Over two hours' excellent enter- taint' ent, embracing almost every mode of swimming, was afforded, the programme comprising some six events, three of which were open handicaps, the remainder being con- fined to members of the club. The entries were numerone, and the races were decided by heats, but towarde the end of the programme several competitors failed to put in an appearance, consequently in one or two instances there was a "swim over." Otherwise the events were well contested, and the close finishes testified to the accurate estimate which the handicappers had formed of the swimming powers of the various competitors. The programme opened with a handi- cap for youths under 15 years of age, distance four lengths of the bath, for which there were seven entries, and it was swum in two heats. Four started in the first heat :—Fred Dobson (8 secs. start), William Dobson (2 secs.), William Farrell (2 secs.), and John Unaworth (scratch). William Dobson proved the winner, Unsworth being a good second. Only two started in the second heat:—Wilfred Gardner (8 secs.), and B. Ray (scratch) ; • and at the third length Gardner, who had been left behind by Ray, a youth almost twice his size, stopped short, when some one urged him on with "Swim it out and chance it," to which he replied in a knowing manner, that created much amusement, "I'm second!" and leisurely completed the last length. In the final heat, however, Gardner retired after doing the second length, and there was a capital race between Ray and Dobson, the former of whom obtained the first prize, a silver chain, and the latter the second, a tourist case, both prizes being presented by Mr. J. Rymer Young. A handicap race for those members of the club who had never won a priza (distance, six lengths) brought out seven of the nine competitors who had entered, and the first heat was won by S. Mather (scratch), Harry Potter (4 secs.) 2; the second heat resulting as follows: 1, J. Pemberton (2 secs.); 2, J. Cunningham (8 secs.) Mather succeeded in obtaining the first place in the final heat, the prize being a writing desk, presented by Mr. Thomas Morris ; and Cun- ningham carried off the second prize, a field glees, given by Councillor Caldwell. The handicap race for members of the club (distance, six lengths) was a most interesting event. There were fifteen entries, but only ten started, and these were reduced to seven by the heats, which were won by the following : I First : 1, Fairfield Turner, (scratch) ; 2, Arthur Howard, (3 secs.). Second: 1, George Grounds, (3 secs.); 2, John Allen (scratch.) 'Third: 1,. W. T. Jenkinson (2 secs.) who "swam over." Fourth: 1, A. Barlow (5 sece.) ; 2, H. Sutton (scratch.) Barlow went ahea lin the final and won easily, but there was an exciting struggle between F. Turner and H. Sutton, two splendid swimmers, for second place. Turner, a strongly built young fellow, just managed to o'etain the victory, beating Sutton by a stroke. The first prize for this race was a set of silver studs and sleeve-links, presented by the Baths Committee, and the second a photograph album, the gift of Alderman Davies. For the open handicap race (20 lengths,) there were eighteen entries, but the event proved a somewhat tame affair in consequence of competitors absenting themselves. In the first heat, A. Howard (2 secs.) had a "swim over ; " only two started in the second heat, J. Carrington (8 secs.) and William Thomas Jenkinson (2 secs.), the former retiring after going two-thirds of the distance; and the third , heat resulted in a " go-as-you-please " contest b:tween W. Thornton (12 secends) and George Grounds (14 seconds), the former of whom won; while of the three who started in the fourth heat only H. Sutton (scratch) swam the distance, J. O'Neil (18 secs.) and J. Dunbobbin (14 secs.) retiring when they had completed ten lengths. Sutton won in the final by two lengths, Howard beating Jenkinson by half a length, although it was obvious that Jenkinson could have taken second place had he exerted himself. The first prize was a handsornephotograph album, presented by the Mayor (Councillor Crosfield), the second being a gent's umbrella, given by Councillor Mackie, and the third a silver medal. Much amusement was created in the hurdle race handicap, confined to members (distance four lengths), by the manner in which the competitors cleared the "hurdle." Some of them went over it splendidly, but others touched now and again,and Cunningham somehow never could get his feet clear of the obstruction. Still with 10 secs start of the scratch man, Jenkinson, he won the first heat; F. Turner (scratch) swam over in the secondl heat ; A. Barlow (5 secs.) was first in the third, and S. Mather (5 secs.) first in the fourth heat. In the final con- test Barlow easily carried off the first prize, an American repeating clock, presented by Sir Gilbert Greene'', and Mather obtained the second prize, a military case of brushes, presented by the captain of the club (Mr. A. M. Smart). The last event was a clothes' racehandicap (four lengths) and ten of the sixteen who had entered started. But as the com- petitors were dressed in closely fitting garments, and minus shirts, waistcoats, and shoes, the race could not be con- sidered a fair test of what they would be able to do in an emergency. The heats were won by J. Allen (1 sec.), G. Grounds (3 secs.), F. Turner (scratch), and W. T. Jenkin- son (2 secs.), the latter's sole opponent giving up after the first length because he found his clothes "too heavy." Turner won the first prize, a gold horse shoe pin, presented by the club, by a yard, and Grounds took the second, a walking stick, beating Jenkinson by half a length. During the evening Miss A. J. Catiey gave an interesting entertain- ment, the more difficult feats including swimming back- wards, then with a glass of water on her head, and next with hands and feet tied together. The display was varied with a dive through a hoop of fire, and a sensational trick with a sack, in which she was tied and dropped into the water, and from which, after a brief period of suspense, she rose freed from the sack. Her performances were much ap- preciated, and she was frequently loudly applauded. Mr. Smart (the captain) gave a floating exhibition, and, with the assistance of Mr. H. Potter, illustrated the best means of saving life. Prier to the concluding race, Councillor Frederick Monks proposed a vote of thanks to the club for the excellent entertainment they had given. He remarked that he,need say little about the advantages of being able to swim- It was a useful art, and certainly afforded a vast amount of pleasure to those who practised it. Athletic exercises were desirable, and he for one could not help but feel glad when. he saw that the young men of the present day were paying more attention to athletic exercises than they (lid when he was a lad. The swimming they had seen that night was certainly excellent as compared with what it was 30 or 4C yers ago. Thirty years ago they had a most excellent swimmer in Warrington, and he did not know any man equal to him; he was one of the best swim- mers he ever saw. He did not know that he had seen any- thing tbat night to equal the swimming of the late Mr. Jahn Fitchett Marsh, to. whom he referred. He had seen Mr. Marsh jump in the bath and undress himself there—a trick which he had not seen per- formed that night. However, there had been one trick shown which he thought, in the interests of humanity,

div.head: HP, EXAMINEE, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 1 1883.
div.p: HP, EXAMINEE, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 1 1883.

should be dispensed with, and that was the trick practise,!' by Miss Catley in the sack. With that exception the en tertainment had been one which commended itself to their judgment, and in many respects to their support. He ex- pressed his pleasure at seeing so many young men present and asked the spectators to show to the club their hearty re- cognition of the entertainment they had given. (Loud ap- plause.) —Councillor Whittle (president of the club) acknowledged the compliment, and observed that in future they would not have any dangerous performances. He th aught the trick was rather too much for Miss Catley to lundertake, and did not like to see it himself. They would try to give a better entertainment next time, and if possible in a better bath. (Applause.)—The prizes were distributed , at the conclusion of the successful gala by the President It should be added that the bath had been specially decorated with flags by Messrs. H. Sutton and H. Potter, and that the following were the officials who had charge of the arrangements, which were, on the whole, well c trriett : out :—Managing Committees A. M. smart, J. %V. Bouchier. lA. Howard, H. Potter, and Ll. Sutton ; handicappers. Messrs Smart and Bradshaw; starter, Mr. E. Wallington; an-I referee, Mr. J. C. Whittle. Officers: president, Mr. Coun- cillor Whittle; captain, Mr. A. M. Stuart; treasurer, Mr. ki. B. Poulson; and hon. secs., Messrs. T. A. and J. H. button.

ODIWELLOWSHIP AT WARRINGTON. On Saturday a number of the members of the Grand Lodge, Liverpool Independent Order of Oddfellows, includ- ing Prov. G.M. William Williams, Prey. C.S. H. Hughes, P.P.G.M.'s Howard, Bowler, Cooper, Tunstall, and ether P.G.'s, paid a visit to the Prince of Wales Lodge, Warring- ton. Prey. G.M. J. Emson, D.P.G.M. Domville, Prov. C.S.J.T. Perry, and other Warrington brethren met the visitors at the station and conducted them to .the Park, the Parish Church, and other places of interest in the town, afterwards to Bro. P.G. Maguire's White Hart Dining Rooms, where they were entertained by the Warrington brethren to a substantial tea, to which about 40 sat down. After tea the members adjourned to the lodge room, at Bro. G. Riley's, Rope and Anchor.—P.G.M. John Emson occupied the P.G.'s chair, and D.P.G M. Domville the V.G.'s.—The usual loyal and 0 idfellows' toasts were given, and drunk in the usual manner.—Bro. C. S. Hteines (Liverpool district), in responding to the toast of the Ind, - pendent Order of Odelfellows, said that very few words need come from him with reference to their noble order, because he was well satiified in Warrington they had brethren in connection with the Or'cler who posted them- selves up with regard to the proceedings, prosperity, and work of their great institution. The, e was no question that so far as the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows were concerned they might safely say it was one of the noblest organizitions for the encouragement of thrift and providing for that period when sickness or old age overtook them; and he was of opinion that their society would progress far more in the future than it had done in the past. They could only speak of the organizetion from some 70 years ago, when, from a few meeting together in Salford, a society had sprung up which was now possessed of six millions of 'money, besides having paid to those who required it in sickness, &c, hundreds of thousands every year. He was very much struck by the way in which they bad been received by the Warrington brethren, and it proved to him that the princi- ples inculcated by their society were well appreciated by the Warrington brethren. In conclusion he said he felt sure the society would grow and remain an honour to the country.—P.P.G.M. WIIITAAM' in proposing" Our Visiting brethren," said the toast he had to propose was one that represented a large amount of good-will amongst htethren. It was really the Past Grands Lodge, of Liverpool, which embraced a larger scope than the Liverpool brethren. In visiting lodges they inculcated those grand virtues of friend- ship, love, and truth; but they added more than that, for, by members exchanging opinions with each other they arrived at what was for the geed of their society. If when they met in their lodges they had not discussed those things which • go to mike up a friendly society they would never have processed as they had done. They met to discuss points of business, and were constantly looking forward towards improvement. It was all very well to take the past to guide them in the future; but they must look forward to improving the lodze, the district, and the unity. By brethren in one district visiting those in another there must be ventilation of opinions, and this must mean prosperity to the Order.— P.P.G.M. Wins (Liverpool), in reepending, apologised for the absence of the N.G of the Past Grands Lodge. He could assure them when he heard of the reception they had had at Warrington he (the N.G.) would only be inure sorry he had not been able to be present. It had been a great pleasure for them to be present, and if they had only come to visit the grand old church it would have repiid them for their visit. With respect to the P.G.s Lodge, it did not only consist of the best heads, but it consisted of the best hearts, and they did all they could to further the interest of their own and other districts.—P.P.G.M. TUNSTALL, in proposing the toast of "The Prince of \Vales Ledge," said it was the toast of the lodge under whose dispensation and auspices they now sat. They had received at their bands one of the most cordial receptions one brother could give to another. He presum.d that the lodge was now in a flourishing condition, and that it was a fair sample of the lodges in Warrington. He spoke at some length on the advisability of a scheme of extended benefits, and expressed the hope that it could be grasped by the unity as a unity scheme, as he was satisfied then that the usefulness of the society would be greatly ex- tended.—P.G. Wadsworth, secretary, in responding to the toast, said they had 167 good members on their hoeke, and that they were worth at the present time over £1,000. Other Oddfellowship toasts were given and responded to, and during the evening songs and recitatiens were given by P.G. Riley, P.P.G M. Potter, P.G. Mollineaux, P.P.G.M. Whitham, P.P.G.M. Cooper (Liverpool), P.P.G.M. Bowler (Liverpool), P.P.G.M. Tunstall (Liverpool), dzc.; and a very pleasant evening was snent.
POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. BATITBDAY.—There was no business for disposal. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (oouneilior Oro;field), and Mr. J,hn Naireiough. _

ON THE DOWNWARD COURSE. —John ns, 21 years of age, was fined 10s and costs, or 14 days, for being drunk and disorderly. This was the prisoner's 13th appearatice. DRUNKEN MILITIAMAN.—Thomas Rolland, a Militiaman sta‘ ioned at Orford Barracks, was fined ss. and costs, or seven days' imprisonment, for being drunk and disorderly; an 1 also ordered to pay Is. 6d damage for breaking a window, the pro- -o—ix of Richard Kilshall, licensed victualler, Iforsemarket- , street.

A BAD CHARACTER —Louisa Cooper was fined ss. and costs. or seven days' iinprisonment in default, for being guilty ut idecency, and assaulting P.O. Shaw, in Queen-street. LATEST NEWS.

THE MERSEY TIINNEL.—Since the report presented to the annual meeting of shareholders the progress made to- wards the completion of the tunnel has been very satisfac- tory. Colonel Beaumont's boring machine has passed the very bard stratum of rock which for some weeks retarded its progress, and is at work upon a variety of the sandstone more easily dealt with. In the last fortnight 67 yards have been excavated, leaving 683 yards still to be passed through before the extremities of the two headings are united. At the present rate this would be accomplished in 20 or 21 weeks. In all other respects the undertaking is progressing equally well. Having driven an adit on the level of the floor of the tunnel in advance of the excavation of the whole section, and then making a chamber at the end of the adit, the contractor is enabled to work on from that point, just getting four faces to work upon—two on the Liverpool and two on the Birkenhead side. All these four faces are under the full tidal flow of the Mersey, far beyond the landing-stage on either side, but the drainage headings, one of which is being driven by the boring machine, are in advance of the main tunnel.—Liverpool Mercury.

BOARDS OF GUARDIANS AND EMIGRATION.—The Local Government Board has just issued a circular dealing with emigration by which the doubts recently expressed respect- ing the powers of guardians of the poor to expend the rates on the emigration of poor persons will be dispelled. The document says :—" The present state of the law on the sub- ject may be thus described. Expenditure for emigration has in the case of unions become a common fund charge. The written concurrence of the guardians of the parish, for- merly necessary in unions, is, therefore, no longer r(quired. Excepting in the case of orphan or deserted children under le years of age guardians of unions can expend money in the emigration of any poor person residing therein, whether actually in receipt of relief or not. With the-latter excep- tion the guardians of a separate parish can expend money on the emigration of any poor person residing therein, who is settled in such parish or irremovable therefrom, whether in receipt of relief or not." Dealing with the cases of orphan or deserted children, the circular says :—" In the cases of orphan or deserted children, chargeability is necessary. The restriction of the 13th arid 14th Victoria, cap. 101, sec 4, to orphan or deserted children having no settlements or whose settlements are unknown, is superseded, and the section is applicable to all orphan or tlesert_d children under 18 years , of age if chargeable."
